The upgraded sand policy was announced by the Maharashtra state government on Saturday, with an anticipated annual revenue of approximately Rs 765 crores.


The director, department of mines and geology entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on January 4, this year with M/s MSTC Ltd, a Central government undertaking to select the eligible agency to undertake sand mining, storage and sales for a period of two years in a transparent and impartial manner.


This upgraded new policy will provide several facilities to customers, including opportunity to check the quality of the sand directly at the ramps, tie up the money at the reach of their choice and take the required quantum of sand in the vehicle they have set up. There will be same price at each reach across the state and a price with upper ceiling is determined regionally based on distance.
Crime branch provided a false crime chart of the accused to the court. Domestic Violence case and Challan Case too included in Crime Chart by SIT to oppose Anticipatory Bail

Nagpur Commissioner of Police Amitesh Kumar has invoked the stringent Maharashtra Prevention of Dangerous Activities (MPDA) Act against Amol Khorgade, alias Guddu, a prominent sand smuggling kingpin. This marks the first use of the amended MPDA Act in Vidarbha.

Deputy CM Devendra Fadnavis had earlier directed the police to take strong action against the sand mafia. Investigations revealed that Khorgade and his associates used fake Electronic Transit Passes (ETPs) to illegally supply sand, causing significant revenue losses. So far, 32 individuals, including Khorgade, have been arrested in this case, and assets worth Rs 5 crore have been seized.

Anil Deshmukh, Home Minister of Maharashtra, along with state guardian minister Nitin Raut, carried out unannounced inspections at the sand ghats in Nagpur district on Tuesday (in July 2020) in response to reports of unauthorized mining activities.

The Deulgaon Raja region in Buldhana district witnessing the unlawful extraction of sand, which is causing a significant loss in revenue for the government. In response to this issue, a protest has been initiated, and the Shivsena taluka chiefs from the Shinde group have commenced a hunger strike in the Khadakpurna river basin.

There has been another incident of firing and bombing in the ongoing conflict between sand mafia in Banka, Bihar. The clash and obstruction over illegal mining and dumping of sand from the Chandan river reached the level of bombing and firing. The clash took place between the people of Navtolia and Majlishpur of Banka.


Both parties are blaming the other regarding the incident. Shortly after the incident, after the arrival of police from several police stations including SDPO, SDM, raids are being conducted to arrest the identified accused while investigating the case.


A violent clash between the two sides over the same issue and an incident of heavy bombing had taken place a month ago in which action was taken to arrest many people, but later both the sides resolved the matter with an agreement.

According to the CAG report, in 14 districts of Bihar, as many as 2,43,811 e-challans were generated using 46,935 unrealistic vehicles having registration number of ambulance, bus, autorickshaws, car and motorcycle shown to be used for transporting minerals ranging from 8 metric ton to 10.89 lakh metric tons.


The performance audit report of the CAG has also detected extensive illegal mining outside the sand ghats and large-scale irregularities in the allotment of sand ghats for mining by the mines and geology department. The report also found mining activities being carried out outside the allotted areas in three districts - Patna, Bhojpur, Rohtas, Banka.


The CAG report highlights many violations and illegalities including - systematic loopholes in approval of coordinates without proper demarcations, irregularities in allotments for sand mining, mining allowed at habitation, in the middle of a high intensity electric tower, agricultural/residential land in place of riverbed, inadequate distance from highway and rail bridge

Upon receiving continued complaints of illegal sand lifting from the Mahandi in Gopalpur area of Cuttack district, a special squad from the police force conducted raids and detained 11 people and seized 7 tracters involved in sand smuggling there.

Despite lockdown, the sand mafia has been exploiting multiple ghats along rivers such as the Mahanadi, the Devi and the Chitropotla in Jagatsinghpur district of Odisha right under the nose of district administration while flouting lockdown guidelines as well. for Sources said the Revenue department had awarded lease of ghats to local bidders for lifting of sand but their lease deed expired just before lockdown and no fresh tender has been invited for the ghats. However, the bidders continue to lift sand illegally taking advantage of the crisis as the administration remains busy in enforcing preventive measures for the pandemic. Jagatsinghpur's Tehsildar even admitted that many bidders, who obtained environmental clearance till June 2020, are yet to submit their mining plans. It is illegal to continue mining without submission of mining plans in time.

The Chandrapur tehsil administration has recently taken extensive measures to combat the activities of the sand mafia. As part of their efforts, they have successfully uncovered a secret location that was being used for the unlawful storage of sand. Additionally, on Saturday, they imposed fines on 14 tractor owners who were found guilty of illegally transporting sand.

13 farmers were killed and several injured when a truck driver (apparently drunk) lost control and rammed into the group of people waiting outside a police station to protest illegal sand mining in Munagalapalem village.

A decapitated body of mugger crocodile was found in Anugul district's area of Satkosia Gorge Sanctuary. Speculations say that either it got caught in a fishing net and hacked later by the fishermen for saving the net or from an impact of blast fishing. Muggers fall in the 'vulnerable' category of IUCN's Red List and are native to freshwater habitats. Activities like illegal fishing, construction of dams and barrages, artificial embankments and sand-mining leading to changes in the river course cause huge irreversible loss of riverine habitat which threatens the existence of this species.

Petition had been filed by two Cuttack residents that indiscriminate extraction of sand through the mechanical means, which was not permissible in law, was leading to degradation of the Mahanadi riverbed. The sand mining leaseholder had made gross violations by allegedly pressing into service three earthmovers and more than 200 heavy vehicles for the sand mining and transportation operations. The Eastern Zone Bench of National Green Tribunal (NGT) ordered the Odisha government to use satellite imagery for monitoring the volume of sand extracted and transported from the Mahanadi riverbed. It also asked for keeping tabs on the extraction and transportation by using CCTV cameras and GPS on vehicles and ordered for the study on annual replenishment of sand in the area.

description: Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB) proposed environmental public hearing for sand ghats in Vidarbha through virtual platform. The administration of Nagpur has earned a revenue of Rs 11.55 crore by auctioning a total of 15 sand ghats in 2018-19. However, the highest bidders took possession of only 11 sand ghats.

In Jagatsinghpur district, illegal sand mining has become a routine activity, violating National Green Tribunal (NGT) directives. Numerous vehicles, including tractors, trucks, and tippers, are used daily for clandestine sand lifting, allegedly with the backing of revenue officials and some politicians. This illegal activity is causing severe soil erosion along the banks of the Mahanadi River, particularly affecting the Tirtol, Raghunathpur, and Kujang blocks. The river banks are eroding rapidly due to unauthorized sand quarrying, which has significant negative impacts on thousands of residents in riverside villages who depend on the river's ecosystem for their livelihoods.


Despite the NGT's ban on the use of illegal machines for sand mining, these are being freely utilized. For instance, ARSS Infrastructure Private Ltd, contracted by the government for the Haridaspur-Paradip railway project, is using JCB machines to extract sand from the Kaladip area near the Mahanadi River. The construction company has requested permission to mine 63,000 cubic meters of sand from this area, with plans to excavate 21,000 cubic meters monthly over three months. However, ARSS is reportedly mining sand from 31 acres instead of the permitted 6.45 acres, resulting in government revenue loss. The NGT prohibits the use of heavy machinery for sand lifting to protect natural topography and prevent river course changes. Local villagers and officials have expressed concerns over these practices, fearing ecological damage and alterations to the river's course. Kujang Tehsildar Basudev Satpathy has denied irregularities but assured action if the agency is found mining beyond the permitted area. Attempts to contact ARSS officials have been unsuccessful.

### Summary of the Situation in Kendrapara:


In Mahakalapada block of Kendrapara district, women-led local residents halted illegal sand mining by the sand mafia near the Mahanadi River, detaining sand-laden vehicles. They protested after authorities ignored their complaints of illegal sand lifitng, fearing damage to bridge pillars nearby and village roads from the heavy machinery and vehicles. Such illegal sand mining, a lucrative business for influential locals, has caused law and order issues in their villages. Tehsildar Manas Ranjan Tripathy reported that several illegal quarries have been closed and stressed the need for environmental clearance, with police directed to act against the sand mafia.

In Jagatsinghpur, the erosion of the Mahanadi river embankments has become a significant concern for villagers. The primary causes of this erosion are the lifting of sand and earth, as well as the establishment of brick kilns along the embankments of the Mahanadi, Paika, and Chitrotola rivers in Tirtol, Raghunathpur, and Kujang blocks. Illegal sand mining, often supported by local politicians and revenue officials, exacerbates the problem.

Residents of Tirtol block report that the embankment near Jhulababa Math has collapsed, resulting in the loss of trees like sal, jackfruit, mango, cashew, and casuarina. They fear that further erosion could lead to more damage. The embankment has collapsed multiple times since its construction, causing anxiety among the locals.

A 400 m length and 250 m width of the embankment have already been damaged, and the 700 m nearby Taladanda canal is at risk. An engineer from the Irrigation department attributes the lack of maintenance to a shortage of funds and has requested the Revenue department to curb illegal sand extraction.

Tirtol Tehsildar Sujata Patra mentioned that the State Government has leased sand lifting rights to contract agencies and that measures are in place to monitor and penalize violators.

In Jagatsinghpur, rampant illegal sand mining has led to severe river erosion along the Mahanadi, endangering both land and lives. The sand mafia's activities remain unchecked by the district administration, posing significant threats to local communities. A 70-year-old woman, Sakhi Behera, was critically injured after protesting against illegal sand mining, allegedly attacked by Lokanath Behera and others, including local officials. 


Her son filed an FIR against the attackers, accusing them of violence and making anti-Dalit remarks. The local sarpanch denied the charges, claiming the sand was being used for house construction under a government scheme, leading to conflicts. 


Despite these incidents, illegal sand extraction continues unabated, with heavy machinery being used to remove sand daily, increasing the risk of river course changes and land erosion, causing panic among villagers. The authorities have registered a case and are investigating the matter.

In Cuttack, the flood protection embankments of the Mahanadi and its tributaries, Luna, Chitroptala, and Birupa, have weakened due to river erosion. While the embankments haven't breached yet, multiple leaks (pipings) have emerged, causing panic among residents of Cuttack Sadar, Salepur, Nischintakoili, and Mahanga blocks. Over eight leaks have been identified along the Luna river embankments, allowing floodwater to seep into nearby canals.

Locals, alongside Water Resources department officials, are working to address a significant leak on Luna's right embankment at Damodarpur. Similarly, efforts are underway to control leaks on Luna's left embankment at Badathakana and Sankilo. A major leak has also formed on Chitroptala's left embankment at Nahalpur, a site of previous breaches.

Residents express concern over the unstable condition of the embankments, fearing potential breaches with additional floodwater. The erosion is attributed to inadequate maintenance and the heavy vehicle traffic transporting sand, which has further weakened the embankments. Assistant Executive Engineer Akshya Kumar Mallik stated that efforts are ongoing to repair the leaks and reinforce vulnerable points.

Illegal and unsustainable sand mining in the Mahanadi River across Cuttack, Kendrapara, and Balasore in Odisha is severely impacting local communities, causing soil erosion and heightened flood risks. Villages like Uttarkul, Babujang, Manijang, Mahammadpur in Cuttack, and Tendakuda in Kendrapara are particularly affected, with 200 feet of floodplain eroded recently, weakening embankments.

In Balasore, riverside villagers near the Subarnarekha River also fear flooding. Villagers report that illegal sand mining has washed away protective trees, and heavy rains have raised river water levels, exacerbating flood threats. Despite temporary measures like sandbagging by the district administration, villagers demand a permanent solution.

Locals allege that the sand mafia, supported by political leaders and revenue officials, continues illegal operations even after lease expirations, altering river courses and destroying floodplains. Some have lost agricultural land to erosion, and there are fears that homes and farmland will soon be submerged. Authorities are taking emergency steps to address erosion using wooden piles and sandbags.

description:
In Cuttack, during the lockdown, sand mafia and unauthorized brick kilns have intensified their activities, exploiting rivers and increasing the threat of COVID-19 spread. Illegal sand mining is rampant along the banks of the Mahanadi, Kathajodi, Chitrotpala, Luna, Devi, and Birupa rivers. Unauthorized brick kilns operate in Cuttack Sadar, Nischintakoili, Mahanga, Kantapada, and Niali blocks, defying lockdown orders.

The sand mafia secretly lifts sand at night, transporting it across the district. Despite locals reporting this to police and revenue officials, no action has been taken. Some officials and activists have faced assaults by the mafia. Social activist Sanjay Routray was seriously injured for protesting illegal sand mining at the Devi river, and a mechanic died in an accident involving a sand-laden tractor where he was trying to check the tyre pressure of a sand-laden tractor.

Residents urge the district administration to halt these illegal activities immediately.

Residents from Gavier, Dumas, Bhimpore, Magdalla and, Vata villages urged the district collector to allow them to mine sand from the river bank.  After the weir-cum-causeway had been built, water flow to a portion of the Tapi had been restricted that resulted in issues in their fishing activities. This was also an issue for the Gujarat Maritime board since they had to dredge that area for transport.

In Cuttack district, illegal sand mining is rampant as the sand mafia exploits riverbeds before the monsoon. Using heavy machinery, they lift sand from the Mahanadi river system and stockpile it on rented agricultural land for future sale. This activity violates government guidelines, with local tehsildars failing to enforce regulations, leading to significant revenue loss for the state.

The use of heavy equipment has disrupted water flow, created large craters, and eroded river embankments. Overloaded trucks transporting sand damage roads and cause accidents, with a recent incident resulting in the death of a 52-year-old man. Despite official claims of enforcing regulations, around 30 additional illegal sand sites are believed to be operating beyond the 63 officially sanctioned ones. The district administration has instructed tehsildars to curb these activities, but enforcement remains inadequate.

The government made a strategic decision to offer sand at a low cost to the general public in the state. Under this new policy, the administration claimed that sand would be available for Rs 600 per brass. 


Despite the announcement, sand remained unaffordable in the district. Consequently, there was an increase in smuggling of sand and other minor minerals through illegal channels. In response to this situation, the first sand depot in West Vidarbha has been established in Mangrul Dastgir, Amravati district. The inauguration of the sand depot in Mangrul Dastgir has paved the way for the public to access sand at a highly reasonable price.

The tender process was conducted for 14 sand depots, out of a total of 44 sand ghats, that were designated for the Amravati district. However, only the sand depot located at Jalgaon Mangrul was ultimately commissioned.

description: The Uttarakhand government plans to mine riverbeds extensively for revenue, raising concerns about environmental damage.  Forest department's action against sand mafia in Morena - firing by the forest department on the sand miners in one of the raids / investigations. Rajasthan High Court reprimands the Bundi police for a shoddy probe into an illegal sand transportation and mining case, and handed over the investigation to CBI. It authorised the central agency to look into similar cases, involving sand mafia active in Chambal and Banas rivers, in which FIRs have been registered. Scale: Sand is being extracted from Sanjeev area of ​​the district, Kachhari Pahat near Nahargarh police station by putting machines fitted on big boats, big pumps and submersibles on the water of Chambal. With the new sand mining policy in place, the Madhya Pradesh government is expected to earn almost Rs.600 crore in revenue compared to Rs. 69 crore in year 2018-19. 43 districts of MP have sand mines. The revised list stands at 1438 sand mines out of which 400 are new mines.


Sand mining lease in the state will now be allotted for three years — this is up from the one-year lease period effective until last year. The rationale behind this decision is to ease the sector from getting into the lease process every year.


In the new mining policy, the government has banned storage and sale of sand within two kilometers from a mine. And also, only the licensed contractors or ones having a mining lease would be allowed to sell sand within 50 kilometers from any sanctioned sand quarry. These restrictions would not be applicable for major cities, including Bhopal, Indore, Gwalior and Jabalpur.


The policy will continue with the state government’s directive for a complete ban on mechanized mining from the quarries along the Narmada.


Under the new policy, sand leasing and mining rights from gram panchayats would be withdrawn. It also stresses on deploying local laborers in the quarries. It states that sand mining, loading and storage from quarries having an area up to five hectares shall be done by the committee of local laborers.

67 sandmining activity units were shut down by the Gujarat High court. These activities had continued without the renewal of the leases. The units were in Gir sanctuary.  Gujarat Forest department submitted that 67 units should not be given an NOC, No Objections Certificates for mining on the banks of river Shetrunji which is in the Gir Sanctuary.  The order was passed in response to a PIL filed by a Surat city citizen who alleged that the sand mining activity was a cause of threat to the wild animals like, Asiatic lions, Bears, hyenas and, golden jackals  present in the sanctuary.

In UP, constable Rohit Kumar Pancholi, 24, was killed while attempting to stop a tractor-trolley involved in illegal sand mining in Farrukhabad district. A complaint had been lodged against 5 people, Pradeep Yadav and Bhupendra Yadav- the two suspects were shot in the leg during the encounter.


In Bihar, constable Deepak Kumar, 29, was run over by a tractor in Aurangabad during a routine check for illegal sand miners. Tractor driver Ramta Singh and tractor owner Dharmendra Yadav had been arrested.


These deaths are not isolated - at least 11 people have been killed across the country since 2023 for exposing or acting against illegal mining operations. On June 6, the body of 25-year-old tractor driver Avanish Kumar was found buried in a sand mound in Bihar's Begusarai. On November 14 last year, sub-inspector Prabhat Ranjan was similarly crushed to death by the sand mafia in Jamui.

The National Green Tribunal banned illegal extraction of minor minerals through mechanized mining in Gonda and Faizabad districts of Uttar Pradesh. A bench headed by NGT Chairperson Justice Swatanter Kumar ordered that there should be no mining activity within 50 meters from the end of the railway track on Mankapur in Faizabad and 150 meters from railway or any other bridges. The tribunal passed the judgement on the plea filed by Lok Sabha MP Kirti Vardhan Singh from Gonda.

It will be manufactured through overburden, rejects and waste boulders and stones lying in quarries or mines. The demand for sand in the state for construction business is around 7.5-8 crore cubic meters in a year whereas the state is only  producing 3 crore cubic meters in a year.

During illegal extraction of sand from Virma river in Mahoba district, Uttar Pradesh, a man named Ghanshyam lost his life when a large mound of sand collapsed on him. After two long hours, the fellow laborers were finally able to pull him out. Ghanshyam was rushed to the hospital where he was declared dead. The family of the deceased blocked the road in protest and demanded for the arrest of tractor driver involved in illegal extraction of sand. The police ensured the grieving family and registered a case against the tractor driver.

1.6 Cr worth of goods and equipment found in a racket carried out for illegal sand mining after a drone survey carried out by the Banaskantha geology department. A penalty of 10 lakhs will be recovered from the offenders.

Commissioners appointed by the National Green Tribunal (NGT) submitted a report on illegal sand mining in four districts of Madhya Pradesh within the Sardar Sarovar Project's submergence area. The report, based on field inspections in December and January with activist Medha Patkar, highlighted violations of environmental norms in Barwani, Dhar, Alirajpur, and Khargone districts.


- In Nimbola and Bhogava (Dhar district), two sand mining leases were granted to Shiva Corporation, but officials could not identify the mining areas, with no boundaries or maps available.

- In Gogowa and Mahapura (Dhar district), there were clear signs of illegal sand mining, and local officials were unaware of the allotted areas.

- In Balgoan (Khargone district), illegal mining was ongoing without permissions.

- In Alirajpur district, three sand mines were found on the river bed of the Hathni River, with boats using heavy pumps to extract sand.

- In Pendra village (Barwani district), miscreants obstructed the inspection by digging the road and placing bushes, but the team managed to continue their inspection after removing the blockage.

The Madhya Pradesh High Court extended the stay on all sand mining operations in the Sardar Sarovar Project (SSP) affected areas until July 1. This decision follows a petition by the Narmada Bachao Andolan (NBA) and an earlier stay granted on May 6. The court ordered district collectors to provide details about sand mine leases, but they failed to do so satisfactorily. The NBA alleges illegal sand mining in the submergence area. The court has requested further details from various authorities and extended the stay on mining activities.

The Narmada Valley Development Authority (NVDA) claimed in an affidavit to the Indore bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court that no mining activities occur on the land they acquired along the Narmada Valley. This statement was made in response to a petition filed by activist Medha Patkar alleging illegal sand mining in Dhar and Barwani districts. Patkar argued that mining activities without NVDA approval violate a 2012 Supreme Court judgment requiring environmental clearance for mining operations. The court directed the state government to file a reply by September 10, with the next hearing on September 15.

In a crackdown on illegal sand mining in Datia district, Madhya Pradesh, the police raided an underground mining site on Sindh river. Three boats laden with heavy mining equipment including diesel suction pumps and large quantity of illegally mined sand were seized from the spot. Both the mine operator and his brother are listed criminal. 

Madhya Pradesh government does not have any proper guidelines on use of suction pumps for legal mining too.

The article is written by Rahul Singh and Aishani Goswami- the Moving Upstream fellows of Veditum India Foundation who walked along certain parts of river Sindh and documented it through various socio-political and ecological lenses.

The authors narrate a detailed picture of Sindh river which originates in Vidisha district of Madhya Pradesh and finally meets Yamuna in Jalaun district of Uttar Pradesh. The report talks about the water quality and river health of Sindh. As per the official figures, the number of polluted rivers in the country rose to 350 in 2018 where the number was 302 in 2015. 

According to a 2018 report, the water quality of Sindh is within the standard limit of all the three key parameters, namely, Dissolved Oxygen, Biochemical Oxygen Demand and Faecal Coliform. A major reason for it could be the lack of industrial hubs along the river. The most populated town on Sindh is Dabra whose population is 2.37 lakh. Agriculture and livestock rearing are major source of livelihoods. 

Madhya Pradesh ranks third in the country for the most number of polluted river sections. Out of the 22 polluted river sections of MP, none of them are on Sindh. 

But, the scale of illegal sand mining is ringing alarm for the ecological health of Sindh.

The report highlights the issue of rampant illegal sand mining being happening on Sindh river across the Datia district of Madhya Pradesh. In addition to the sand extracted from the legal sand mines there's an even larger ecosystem of illegal sand mining flourishing under the nose of district administration. As, the sun goes down, scores of trucks and tractors line up to start transporting illegally mined sand from the forested land. Mechanized sand mining is being carried out flouting all the norms, both in the legal as well as illegal mines. Deep pits had been dug in the river channel which had led to several deaths in the region due to drowning.

The interstate bridge on Ken river bridging the gap between Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh is under threat from sand mining being carried out in its vicinity. Excessive mining adjacent to its pillars has exposed its plinth endangering the structure. Sand was being mined to the depth of 3 meters to 4 meters right beneath the pillars of the bridge. Mining has been stopped in all the sand mines located near the bridge. There will be no mining 500 meters on both sides of the bridge.

In reply to NGT in a case on illegal sand mining, the Madhya Pradesh government had admitted of the fact that illegal sand mining is happening on the Ken river in Panna district. The government also informed the green tribunal that cases of illegal extractions had been registered against 11 violators.

The central bench of the NGT also directed that no authority/court should release vehicles and equipment found involved in illegal mining or transportation of minerals without referring the matter to the Tribunal and obtaining the order regarding the same.

The sand mafia from Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh deployed a large number of earthmoving machines and dug out sand in large quantity before the June 15 ban comes into effect in view of the impending monsoon. Mounds of almost 4,000 truck-loads of sand had been dumped near the Dhasan river. Temporary bridges were constructed to facilitate the transportation of sand.

Sand mining is a big political issue in Madhya Pradesh. From politicians to police, everyone had been held responsible for being complacent and involved in corrupt practices.

The GPS tracking system was installed in Hitachi machines in leased areas as a way to check for unauthorized activities. A raid was carried out by the team of Vadodara Mines and Minerals department and items worth 1 Cr. were recovered from the accused. 


The leased Hitachi machines will be installed with GPS tracking in the Sayar-Nareshwar area. If machines without this system are used, legal action will be taken against them.

Police seized a poclain and tractor involved in illegal sand mining. The villagers had complained about the mining and even made a video that went viral on social media. The firm involved had a tender for sand mining but was not mining in the designated place.
A dispute turned violent over extracting sand from a field in Tularampur village. The police have registered a case and are looking for the accused.
A resident of Korwadih village was injured in a fight with another villager over extracting sand from the Danro river using a tractor.

"Sand mafia" is very active in the Kusumghatta Nunbil river ghat and is taking dozens of tractors loaded with sand daily. The article alleges the involvement of the local administration. The "mafia" is transporting 150 cft of sand instead of 100 cft even though at 100 cft of sand a challan is issued. This is causing huge losses to the government's revenue.

The article reports on the monsoon ban on sand mining being imposed in Jhansi district, Uttar Pradesh. The ban would be in place from July 1 to September 30. The sand had been already stored in 21 depots which would be made available for the coming months. In total, 1,00,30,000 cubic meter sand is in stores. The administration had asked to remove all sand mining machinery from 18 mining spots in the district.

The Adivasi Ekta Parishad protested against the alleged illegal sand mining in Valod sub-district of Tapi-district that is largely dominated by tribal communities. In a statement to the Gujarat government signed by Lalsinh Gamit asked the government to clarify whether the permission was given to carry out sand mining was given and on what ground. The sand mining activity is causing damage to the environment and the statement asked for the government to take action under PESA Panchayat (Extension to Scheduled areas) Act 1996, since it requires certain areas to be under the tribal self rule.

6 blocks of land will be set up for auction on the bank of river Tapi. These are situated on Kamrej, 25 km from Surat. The auctioning will help generate a revenue of 8.6 crore. This will also put a check on sand prices as they had sky rocketed.

India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT) halted illegal sand mining in the villages of Tondavali and Talashil in Maharashtra State, on India’s west coast. The villages, squeezed between the Gad River and the Arabian Sea, suffer from soil erosion caused by illegal sand mining in the Gad River, and salt water intrusion from rising seas.

This issue stems from illegal sand mining being reported in Bokaro which prompted the NGT  to take action. Section 144 was imposed in the mine areas in Chhatarpur district of Madhya Pradesh. The administration had banned use of heavy machines in the mines. Also, order had been issued prohibiting mining from 9 pm to 7 am. It has also barred people from carrying arms in the mining areas of the district. Tensions are also brewing in adjoining districts of Banda and Panna. Both the BJP and Congress are throwing allegations at each other of creating sand cartels.

Acting upon the NGT's order (OA-673/2018), the government had sprung into action. In four districts of Bundelkhand, namely Lalitpur, Jhansi, Jalaun and Hamirpur- 100m buffer area would be demarcated on both the banks of Betwa river. On this 350 km stretch, any sort of construction, encroachment, commercial or polluting activities and sand mining would be banned. The entire stretch would be declared as a flood plain zone/ no development zone. 

In total, 134 sand mines would get closed (125 in Hamirpur and 9 in Jalaun). According to the revenue department, the annual royalty which Hamirpur and Jalaun districts receive is around 200 crore and 170 crore Indian rupees annually. 

Also, on the other side of Bundelkhand, there's a mixed feeling about this. The sand mining ban on Betwa would increase the pressure on Ken, Yamuna and Bagen river, turning it into sand mining hotspot but the mine owners there are also worried about increased competition in securing mining leases.

In the reply to an RTI filed by Romel Sutariya, which says that Gujarat government is not complying to directions set by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court had asked to restore the land to villages that they belong to.

The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has asked the Karnataka state government not to allow leaseholders to use heavy machinery in carrying out sand mining in river beds.

The petitioner (former MLA Sarvabhoum Bagali from Vijayapur) alleged large-scale illegal sand mining at two different sites in the Krishna River Bed in Joldahadgi Village, Devadurga Taluk in Karnataka's Raichur using JCB machines which is against the guidelines issued by the Ministry of Environment and Forests and Climate Change on sustainable sand mining policy.

The Palera road in Nowgong sub district of Chhatarpur had been turned into a hillock and is being used for deposition and storage of sand. The concerned officials when asked were totally unaware of the situation. An application had been submitted by a local named Imran Khan to the collector, seeking action against the mining officer.

The article highlights how the issue of rampant and illegal sand mining fails to become an election issue in the state of Madhya Pradesh. Though the fact being out in open that illegal sand mining is responsible for deteriorating health of rivers like Narmada, Chambal, Betwa, Son, Tapi, etc., yet there's sheer lack of accountability from all the shareholders involved in it. More than 3,000 people have been killed over the past year in accidents with sand-laden tractors and trucks. In the last five years alone, sand mafia gangsters have fired on police at least 150 times in Chambal.

In places like Chambal, it has taken the shape of cottage industry in which a large number of jobless youth get work.

Gwalior-based advocate Raju Sharma, who was asked by the high court to take the issue of saving Chambal Ghariyal Sanctuary to NGT, said, “The government opposed the PIL. There is a lack of political will to stop illegal sand mining as vote banks are involved.”

Legal mining can be resumed in 4 stretches of the Chapora river after the Goa SEIAA approved the proposal at its meeting on October 5 but the SEIAA has asked for further studies to be carried out in two other zones in the Chapora. For the 4 approved zones, sand extraction during the first 3 years will only be at 50% capacity. The Goa SEAC had permitted to resume extraction at the 4 locations after a report from the National Institute of Oceanography.

Union minister for environment, forest and climate change Bhupendra Yadav, on Monday, assured chief minister Pramod Sawant to allow sand mining in coastal regulation zone (CRZ).

State govt urged the Centre to allow sand extraction from sand bars for construction activities as there is a shortage of the commodity due to the ban on its extraction in Goa. CRZ notifications 2011 and 2019 prohibit the extraction of sand in CRZ areas and sustainable sand mining guidelines are framed considering dry riverbed mining in non-coastal parts of the country.

The Goa Coastal Zone Management Authority (GCZMA) has observed that rampant sand extraction along the bank of River Mandovi in the villages of Tiswadi, Bicholim and Ponda talukas has deepened the riverbeds, resulting into erosion of the banks, and is reeling under possible threat of more areas getting eroded. Complaints were also filed with regards to cutting of mangroves & trees without permission, land filling in the river to change land use, permanent and temporary construction of hutments, pucca structures and roads within No Development Zones (NDZ) and Coastal Regulation Zones (CRZ) along the bank of Mandovi River in the three talukas. This has resulted into loss of coconut trees and has incurred loss to the traditional dwellers i.e. farmers and farm workers. It is also learnt from the local people that these activities have affected the habitat of marine life, including 'Khube', shellfish whose number has drastically decreased. Traditional dwellers depending on the harvest of these ‘Khube’ for their livelihood are facing serious problem.

A large amount of sand extraction has been going on in the Ghod river basin in Pargaon for six months under the name of government sand extraction. It has come to the notice of the Gram Panchayat that sand is not being distributed by the concerned contractors as per the rules of the government. Also, sand depot and sand lifting are not done as per rules, sand is not sold by weight, weighing forks are not present, CCTV is not installed at sand depot, number plates are not installed on vehicles transporting sand as per rules.

A delegation of the South Western Railway (SWR) comprising engineers and senior officials conducted an inspection of the foundation of the railway overbridge at Cotta-Chandor in light of speculations that rampant illegal sand extraction may have caused damage to its structure. They found no immediate damage but alert police authorities to keep an eye on any illegal sand mining or transportation activities.

Civil society is requesting district collector to look into the illegal mining happening in the Manganga river, Mhasawad block of the Satara. They are worried about the large scale mechanisation of the process to mine large quantities of sand.

A police team raided an illegal sand mining site in Bhandara district in Maharashtra after decorating their vehicles to pass off as a wedding procession.

The report does not explain much on the case registered, but says Nagpur Range Inspector General of Police KMM Prasanna said the stringent Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act (MCOCA) may be invoked in the case.

The police team executed an elaborate, fake wedding procession to seize 12 tipper trucks, eight excavators and sand, all valued at ₹ 3.6 crore.

The Surat district collector has taken action against M M Infra Buildcon, a company based in Navsari, following complaints of illegal sand mining in the Tapi river at Dumas. The company has been accused of causing significant environmental damage to mangroves, fisheries, and river banks. Specifically, the district collector has ordered M M Infra Buildcon to obtain a no-objection certificate (NOC) from the Coastal Regulatory Zone (CRZ) authority within 15 days. Failure to do so will result in further actions against the company owners.

A team of Ahmedabad rural police’s special operations group (SOG) raided a mining site at Gyaspur near the Sabarmati river, late on Thursday night, after reports emerged of illegal sand mining. The team seized vehicles worth Rs 1.36 crore including 3 earth moving machines, 2 dumpers and 12 tractors with trailers.

description: A ground report of the impact of sand mining in Maharashtra. Vaibhav Pawar, Naib Tehsildar of Umarkhed Tehsil in Yavatmal District, was severely attacked by sand smugglers, resulting in 28 stitches to his stomach. Pawar is among many government officials targeted by illegal sand mining, which also threatens journalists. Illegal sand mining not only deprives the government of revenue but also damages the environment. This BBC Marathi report explores the scope of illegal sand mining in Maharashtra and India, the workings of the illegal sand mining nexus, its environmental impact, and the government's response.

Sand mining is taking place near the riverside villages in many places in Vadodara city district, in which the government is giving permission in some places, but taking advantage of it, sand mafias are running illegal sand mining business by digging indiscriminately. The administrative system has failed to stop it. On the other hand, now the District Collector has issued an order banning public bathing at 23 places on Narmada River, Mahisagar Kantha area villages and Narmada Canal, due to which controversy has arisen.

The banks of rivers Krishna, Warna and Panchganga overflowed due to the unprecedented rainfall submerging hundreds of villages. However, the overflow has other major reasons-

Unchecked construction in the riverbed as well as within the flood line, major sand mining in riverbeds, cutting down of trees, industrial waste flowing into rivers, and an impossible amount of plastic and trash being thrown into the river.


The report mentions loss of lives of about 50 people, due to impact of floods.

A team of Mines and Minerals Department raided illegal sand mining in Mahi river, amid complaints that land mafias who have been stealing minerals for a long time in the stretch of Mahisagar river passing through Anand district have become unruly under the watch of the system

As sand mining activity has increased in the rivers passing through Gandhinagar district, bulldozers have systematically dug the Sabarmati river up to hundreds of feet (80 to 100 ft) and created deep pits in it. Because of this, these water-filled river pits prove to be deadly in monsoons.


Report mentions about deaths due to drowning, but not the exact number.
The Gujarat high court on Wednesday, issued a notice to the state government on a public interest litigation seeking act against illegal sand mining in rivers.

A joint task force consisting of officials from the Revenue Department, Mines, Police, and Regional Transport Office (RTO) has seized 18 dumpers and 43 boats involved in illegal sand mining and transportation along the Narmada River. The operation was organized in response to complaints of land mafia activities in the region

A journalist and cameraman from a Gujarati daily were beaten up by persons allegedly involved in illegal sand mining in the Mahi River.


The victims were admitted to the hospital in wake of the incident.The incident took place on Wednesday morning when the cameraman Pradeep Chaubey and reporter Jigen Vora had gone to Kotna on the banks of Mahi after receiving information about illegal sand mining there.

Due to indiscriminate sand mining, large and deep pits are formed in the rivers and drowning incidents are also happening.


Meanwhile, due to the apprehension of theft of royalties in sand mining, a survey of sand mounds (stocks) raised in Yatradham Nareshwar and surrounding places in Karajan taluka has been conducted by the teams of Mines and Minerals Department of Gandhinagar.


Apart from Karajan in Vadodara district, large-scale sand mining is also being done at Chandod, a pilgrimage site in Dabhoi taluk. Sand mining is also going on near the wells of Mahisagar which supplies water to Vadodara. Recently two youths drowned in Kotna in Mahisagar.

A buzz everywhere that government sand will be available for six hundred rupees; But there was no satisfactory response from the contractors for sand mining and depot. As they could not afford the cost of transportation, people turned their backs on government sand and started buying sand from sand smugglers by paying Rs.350 to Rs.5000 in cash. Meanwhile, as sand mining has been stopped from June 9 to September 30, the district administration has now invited tenders for bringing silt or mixed sand from the river in the name of controlling the flood situation. It approved eight sand depots. Among them, storage of sand mixed with silt has been started at Dahar Budruk Depot.

The High Court of Bombay at Goa had called for reports from the nodal officers designated to keep a check on illegal sand mining. The Goa Rivers Sand Protectors Network submitted to the court a list of 47 complaints made to nodal officers on illegal excavation of sand between December 1 and 31, 2021. The report mentions instances of extensive sand mining in Amona Bridge, Amona and Candola (PWD property), Bhati, and Oxel-Siolim. The High Court had passed comprehensive directions to the government to keep a check on illegal sand mining.

A Thomson Reuters Foundation investigation revealed workers were drowning while illegally mining sand in Vasai Creek. In response, the Maharashtra government promised to end illegal mining along the creek, impose regulations, and provide alternate jobs. Although the industry slowed considerably since the crackdown, poverty and wage difference and immaterialization of rehabilitation policies still drive men risking injuries and even deaths.

The article talks about surprise raids conducted by The Pune district administration on the bank of the Ujani Dam, where they confiscated equipment like suction pipes, electric motors, earth movers and even destroyed equipment such as fibre boats. Sources said the administration had identified similar areas in the district that are vulnerable to illegal sand mining and will carry out checks there in the days following these raids (~27th Jan, 2016).

The Bombay High Court has issued contempt notices to the Goa chief secretary, the director of Mines and Geology, and the director general of police for violating its orders on curbing illegal sand mining in Goa after hearing a petition filed by the Goa River Sand Protectors Network. In December of the previous year, the high court issued direction to the Goa government to regularly undertake patrolling of all stretches of rivers using flying squads. Activists allege that sand mining stopped for a while but resumed again and authorities ignored it.

A royalty inspector with geology and mining department and a hotel manager were booked by the anti-corruption bureau (ACB) in Narmada district for accepting a bribe of Rs 60,000 from a sand contractor.

In the Orsang river passing through the district including Chotaudepur town, sand is being mined illegally. Sand is being loaded illegally in tractors at night where the lease has not been allocated.


The two water works operated by the municipality in Orsang river provides water to the population of 35,000 people of Chhotaudepur town. Around 15 years ago, sand layers were seen around it. Now the water level has gone deep due to the disappearance of sand mining. So in earlier times there was water in the river till the month of May. Now as it ends in the month of March, the people of the town are facing water problems.


Every year sand mining activities are carried out for 8 months except monsoon.

The Comprehensive District Survey Report on river sand mining in South Goa district has unveiled severe environmental impacts on the Zuari River. Compiled with data from government departments and the National Institute of Oceanography (NIO), the report emphasizes urgent intervention to mitigate cumulative effects on the riverine and estuarine ecosystems. Highlighting deleterious consequences, such as erosion, degradation, and saline intrusion, the report underscores the challenges in sustaining sand mining practices. Geomorphological changes including erosion, midchannel deposition, and the formation of new mining pits have been observed, leading to significant riverbed degradation and alterations like bar thinning and sediment accumulation downstream. Over time, the formation of numerous pits and gorges has further disrupted the river and estuary landscapes. Increased salinity in lower estuary areas has damaged traditional embankments, impacting adjacent lands originally used for agriculture and conservation areas. Factors like land subsidence and sediment removal exacerbate these issues. The report presents key recommendations focusing on adherence to sand extraction guidelines, depth restrictions, and the implementation of an Environmental Conservation and Management Plan. It divides the region into four zones based on geomorphology and sensitivity, each with specific recommendations for mitigating impacts and regulating sand mining activities. Highlighting seismic data near critical areas, the report underscores the dynamic nature of the riverine environment and stresses the need for regulated sand extraction practices aligned with Sustainable Sand Mining Guidelines and National Green Tribunal directives. In conclusion, the report emphasizes the imperative of sustainable sand mining practices to safeguard the fragile balance of the Zuari River ecosystem. It advocates for manual extraction methods within designated areas, strict depth limits, and careful monitoring to ensure environmental preservation and long-term sustainability.

description: The Maharashtra Government has initiated steps to rejuvenate 53 highly polluted river stretches in the state, as identified by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB). This includes forming a 'River Rejuvenation Committee' in line with National Green Tribunal (NGT) directions. A Government Resolution (GR) mandates restricting sand mining in these polluted areas and calls for regular monitoring and coordination to reduce pollution. The Regional Officer of Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB) will act as the nodal officer, overseeing a joint control group from various departments to curb illegal sand mining. Maharashtra has the highest number of polluted river stretches in India, with eight located in the Vidarbha region. These rivers include Wainganga, Wardha, Kanhan, Kolar, Pedhi, Penganga, Wena, and Chandrabhaga. The GR outlines a five-stage categorization of the polluted stretches, and efforts to clean and rejuvenate these rivers are supported by the Central Government through financial and technical assistance under schemes like the National River Conservation Plan (NRCP) and Namami Gange.

The revenue department of Pandharpur has undertaken a strike campaign against illegal sand mining and traffic. Tehsildar Sachin Langute informed that the revenue team has destroyed 11 boats used for illegal sand and transportation

In one of the biggest crackdown on sand mining mafias in Chhota Udepur, its district collector raided illegal miners at Suskal village and seized 12 sand excavating machines and 37 trucks. Residents and local politicians have been raising the issue that due to rampant sand mining, the water table in the region has gone down drastically, causing an acute water crisis in the district.
The seized 30 brass stock of illegal sand, stolen (cost 1 lakh 20 thousand rupees) were stored in Mauja Kakadara cemetery while transporting.

The Cabinet approved a proposal to streamline the process related to allotment of licences for traditional sand mining and laterite stone mining in the State. CM Pramod Sawant said that clearance has been received for sand mining in the North Goa district and people could apply for licences. People could also apply for permission with the Directorate of Mines and Geology for quarrying on both, the Comunidade land and the government land with due NOCs, he said.

river: Kulshi / Kulsi, Brahmaputra, Dudhnoi/Manda, Mora Kolohi, Boko
description:
Villagers from Assam and Meghalaya, united by a common cause despite long-standing boundary disputes, are protesting illegal sand mining along border rivers. On November 2, 2024, groups like the Garo Students' Union (GSU) and All Bodo Students' Union (ABSU) rallied in Meghalaya’s North Garo Hills, highlighting the severe environmental damage and livelihood threats caused by unchecked mining. 


Leaders like Dhiraj Hazowary (ABSU) condemned the erosion, riverbank damage, and harm to aquatic life, with particular concern over the Dudhnoi River. Despite earlier complaints in 2023 prompting some action, illegal mining has resumed. The mining threatens habitats for endangered species like the Gangetic dolphin in the Kulsi and Morakolohi rivers. Local leaders are calling for stronger, coordinated action to stop the destruction.

The author writes in detail about the chaotic and abysmal state of the sand mining sector in India. From the multi crore sand mining scam in Punjab to the blood soaked sand mines of UP, it is an open field for the people in power to fill their pockets and run havoc on the social and ecological fabric of countless life sustaining rivers of our country. 

There are no official figures for the amount of sand mined illegally. 

The article highlights some of the latest policy changes surrounding the minor minerals extraction especially sand mining. MoEFCC issued Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines in March 2016. Same year, in May, it amended the EIA Notification 2006 to make environmental impact clearance mandatory for small-scale sand mines. 

But, how much transparency and accountability these policy changes had brought in, remains a hugely debated issue. In pursuance of the 2016 guidelines, the Uttar Pradesh government banned sand mining across the state for July, August and September through an order passed on March 19. But in May, it issued 200 leases to allow mining in all districts, including Etawah, for six months. 

Shortage of human resources is another issue. DEAC consists of 11 experts, including the district magistrate/collector and sub-divisional magistrate, who have to look at the sustainability of sand mines. In Bhind there are 57 sand mining spots. For 11 members, who have other primary responsibilities, going to every mine can be quite difficult.

Sand smugglers attacked revenue officers at Khatkheda Ghat in the Pavani Taluka. Previously, there have been similar attacks on sub-divisional officers in this area. The officers intercepted a truck transporting illegal sand, which led to a confrontation.

It is prohibited to auction the sand of the places where there is a water supply scheme in the river bed, and the use of any machinery is prohibited. Sand can only be mechanically removed. Along with this, it is impossible to hold sand auction this year due to various conditions and regulations from the environment department.


Five teams will be formed in each taluka to monitor illegal sand mining activity.

Three days after the annual seasonal ban on sand mining was lifted, extracted stocks of sand and canoes were seized in a joint raid conducted by authorities on Wednesday.

Sources said that 80 cubic meters of sand and 18 canoes were seized in a joint raid by the mines and geology department, captain of ports (CoP), revenue authorities (Pernem mamlatdar) and Pernem police against illegal sand extraction at Torsem bordering Maharashtra.

Illegal sand mining was being carried out on the banks of Bhima river in Shirapur Hingni division of Daund. When the district administration got information about this, the Baramati Crime Branch and the Quick Action Team seized 31 motor boats blew them up in an explosion,  seized 6 JCB rucks.


Last month, the police had taken major action in Kagaon of Yavat tehsil of Pune district. Here, on receiving information about illegal sand mining from Bhima river, the Crime Branch team raided and recovered goods worth Rs 93 lakh. A case was registered against 12 people in this raid.

Illegal and unplanned sand excavation along the Krishna river in Sangli district has severely impacted the natural habitat of crocodiles. Environmental experts report an increase in crocodile sightings, attributing the problem to the negligence of the state government, district administration, and forest department. Contractors using motorboats for sand digging create noise and disrupt the crocodiles' habitat, forcing them to find new locations for basking and nesting. This has led to a human-crocodile conflict, especially during the nesting season from February to June. Crocodiles have been observed traveling upstream to Karad in Satara district and downstream to Sangli city in search of safe spots. Environmental activists call for strict action against illegal sand mining. The minor mineral department, along with the revenue department, manages sand mining in the district, generating around Rs 50 crore annually from auctioning sand plots in the Krishna river. Previous research by Nikhil Whitaker highlighted the need for a long-term projection of crocodile population growth and the potential for local communities to benefit from crocodile conservation.

Mula riverbed passing through Sakur plateau area of Sangamner taluk, sand smugglers have literally sifted through. Large-scale illegal sand mining is going on here in broad daylight and even in the dark of night. Sand is being transported by various vehicles. But now the revenue department has tightened its belt to stop this illegal sand mining. The roads leading along the river have been dug and Tehsildar Dheeraj Manjare has ordered legal action against the sand smugglers.

The article gives an intro to the India Sand Watch platform - Created by Kolkata’s Veditum India Foundation, India Sand Watch has been designed to become a one-stop destination for those concerned about sand mining in the country, from activists and journalists to researchers and policymakers.

Kuchha roads build around the Narmada were found in the Shuklatirth region of Bharuch. These are used to smuggle sand and other minerals from the river bed. Dholakia, the chairman of Hari Krishna export private ltd. also got a kuchha road built at the river bed that reached his private property.

description: The Vidarbha Economic Development Council (VED) has proposed key recommendations for Maharashtra's new mining policy, including securing environmental clearance before mine auctions, removing upfront royalty payments, and streamlining business processes. These suggestions will be presented at the Mincon-22 conference from October 14-16, held in collaboration with the state's mining department and the Maharashtra State Mining Corporation (MSMC). VED hopes the new policy will incorporate their recommendations and be announced at the event. Key attendees include Union Minister Pralhad Joshi, Transport Minister Nitin Gadkari, and Deputy Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis. VED aims to facilitate private mining and suggests power subsidies for manganese processing to boost regional GST revenue.

Two-thirds of the world's beaches are disappearing due to sand mining, with significant sand loss reported near Mumbai since 2003. The Awaaz Foundation has launched a "Save Our Sand (SOS)" campaign to raise awareness about the issue and urge stricter enforcement of sand mining regulations. The campaign, led by Sumaira Abdulali, uses videos and social media to educate the public and advocate for action against sand mafias. The United Nations Environment Programme will release a report on sand mining, including case studies by the foundation.

More than half a dozen illegal sand mining cases from Jharkhand are going on in the NGT many of which were taken on suo moto cognizance. The JSPCB investiated Seraikela, found evidence of illegal mining by villagers and seized 5 boats. The district has been asked to submit an action report. NGT also took suo moto cognizance of illegal mining in Giridih's sakri river and first hearing of this case was on May 16, 2024. There is a case of illegal sand mining at the Jamshedpur border. NGT asked the JSPCB to submit on report on how sand was being sold despite the ban.

The article highlights the scene of rampant illegal sand mining in the Hamirpur district of UP along the Betwa and Dhasan river. Large scale in stream mining using heavy machines is being carried out in the night hours flouting all environmental norms and NGT's order. Temporary bridges had been built to transport illegally extracted sand. The state is losing significant revenue while the concerned authorities seem helpless.

Two temporary bridges had been bulldozed in morrum mine-24/9. Trucks carrying sand are being checked and fined for carrying illegal sand. Illegally extracted sand is now being seized. The following are the details from some of the mines: 

(a) Morrum mine 23/14: 4516 cubic meter illegal sand

Four children drowned in a deep pit caused by illegal sand mining in the Gevrai tehsil of Beed district on Sunday evening. Locals said illegal sand mining had led to the formation of deep pits along the river banks, and many accidents were taking place at such spots.

The Parbhani police have filed charges of murder, unlawful assembly, and rioting against eight suspects in connection with the death of a young person who passed away four days after being attacked by individuals believed to be part of the sand mafia.

description: The state government plans to utilize drones or unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with advanced cameras to pinpoint areas of illegal sand mining, in accordance with the directives from the central government.

Despite police and mining dept actions, sand "mafia" is not stopping their activities in Dhanbad. They conducted raids and seized several trucks laden with sand, tractors, and an escort car. The DSP of Dhanbad said that these actions against illegal sand mining will continue.

The NGT took suo moto cognizance of a Live Hindustan article about illegal sand mining in Dhanbad and has registered a case. A hearing was held in Delhi in may and the follow-up hearing will be in July, in Kolkata. Despite category 2 sand ghats not being auctioned in Dhanbad for many years, sand is being mined illegally from these ghats and is being sold at a high price.

The ED launched a search into the resident of Punj Singh, business partner of Subhash Yadhav (who was arrested in a Rs 250 crore sand mining scam) in his sand and liquor businesses. The ED is trying to corroborate the trail of incriminating documents found on Yadav's premises. The ED has already arrested 5 people from Dhanbad in this case.

The Central Bureau of Investigation summoned Samajwadi Party president and former Uttar Pradesh chief minister Akhilesh Yadav for questioning in connection with an illegal sand mining case from 2019.

Yadav held the state’s mining portfolio between 2012 and 2013, during which time he once approved 13 mining leases in a single day, the Central Bureau of Investigation had claimed. Existing mining licenses were also renewed despite a ban by the National Green Tribunal on sand mining.

In 2019, the CBI carried out raids at 14 places in connection with a first information report lodged against 11 public servants and politicians.

In the span of two months, the Ahmednagar police have filed charges against 61 individuals in connection with 31 cases of unauthorized sand mining. During their operations, they managed to seize sand, vehicles, and various items valued at a total of Rs 2.8 crore

The state revenue officials took action against a gang involved in illegal sand excavation from Kalyan creek by setting six boats used for sand mining on fire and damaging three suction pumps by submerging them in the creek. Additionally, they seized 656 brass sand, resulting in a total loss of Rs 94 lakh for the accused.

Despite the NGT's ban, sand mining and smuggling is continuing from almost all ghats of Dhanbad district. The authorities are silent. The article describes illegal sand mining happening at a very large scale in the Bagmara and Topchanchi regions.

At the village Bhopamadi, in Movasa Taluka, a raid was carried out by the Rajkot Range Police. There is already an alleged nexus forming between the local administration and the sand mafia, and the raid being done by the Rajkot Police made the claim stronger. 14.45 Cr worth of sand stock was seized along with equipment and vehicles.

The CBI conducted searches at 22 locations in Uttar Pradesh and Delhi-NCR in connection with its probe into an alleged mining scam during the Akhilesh Yadav regime in UP.  Three residences owned by Gayatri Prajapati, the then mining minister were searched in Amethi. As many as 11 locations in Hamirpur, two in Delhi and one in Ghaziabad were also raided. Prajapati is currently in jail in connection with a rape case filed by a woman who claimed he exploited her under the pretext of helping her with a mining lease.

“It was alleged that public servants, in criminal conspiracy with other accused, allowed illegal mining of Minor Minerals in District Hamirpur (UP) during the period 2012-2016,” CBI spokesperson Nitin Wakankar said.

A SPECIAL court sentenced former Uttar Pradesh minister Gayatri Prajapati and two others to life imprisonment in a 2017 rape case.

The case against Prajapati and six others was lodged under IPC provisions relating to rape, attempt to rape, criminal intimidation, intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace among others. Police also invoked charges under POCSO. The victim had alleged that she knew Prajapati, who then held the mining portfolio, and used to visit his two official residences in Lucknow for allotment of a mining lease in her name in Hamirpur district. It was during these visits that she was raped, the woman had said. She also alleged that on one occasion, Prajapati tried to outrage the modesty of her minor daughter.

The absence of auctions for sand ghats in the district has led to rampant illegal sand mining, particularly in the Savner, Kamthi, and Mauda talukas. Political leaders and their associates, allegedly supported by Ministers and MLAs, are exploiting this situation to steal large amounts of sand from the Kanhan and Pench rivers. This has resulted in significant revenue loss for the government and has emboldened sand thieves, disrupting the peace in nearby villages.

Sand is highly sought after for construction purposes. However, it is imperative that sand mining is carried out with the appropriate authorization. Despite this, certain contractors continue to extract sand without prior permission, only seeking approval afterwards. The crucial issue at hand is whether the Nagpur collector will grant them the necessary permission. Conversely, in Gondia, the Collector and his staff are vigilantly monitoring the sand quarries to thwart any attempts of sand smuggling.

The abrupt transfer of Nagpur Rural SP Vishal Anand has generated significant controversy and unrest among Maharashtra Cadre IPS officers and political leaders. Anand's strict enforcement against illegal sand mining, particularly his application of the MPDA against a politically influential figure, appears to have triggered his transfer. This move, influenced by political pressures, has caused unease within the police department and heightened political rivalries, especially with upcoming elections. The transfer, seen as politically motivated, underscores the ongoing tension and distrust between law enforcement and political entities in the region.

A female government official narrowly avoided an assassination attempt by the sand mafia as the driver of a truck, carrying illegally extracted sand, attempted to hit her. The incident took place close to Ghotitok village on the Mansar Tumsar national highway in Nagpur district. Vandana Savrangpatte, the official in question, along with her team from the revenue department, had confiscated eight trucks loaded with illegally mined sand during a regular inspection.

description: The Sand Mafia, in collusion with officials from Nagpur and Bhandara Districts, had been flourishing without any obstacles until now. Nevertheless, the recent ruling from the National Green Tribunal has shaken them to their very foundation. Justice Swatantra Kumar, leading the NGT Bench, emphasized that the ban will be nationwide due to the petition's grave environmental concerns.

Ashish Deshmukh, a former MLA, has lodged a formal complaint with the registrar of the National Green Tribunal (NGT), Suresh Rajurkar, regarding the purported illegal sand mining activities taking place near the prominent ghats of the Kanhan river.


Disclosing the locations to the green court, Deshmukh said that mining is taking place on a large-scale at Khapapeth, Wakodi, Tembhurdoh, Ramdongri, Walni, Rayawadi, Isapur, Rohana and many more river banks aligned with the Kanhan river.


Report mentions about long term adverse impacts of sand mining, including weakening of infrastructure like bridges, trucks carrying sand damage roads, impact on river health and ecosystem and threat of water crisis.

Despite the sand ghats in various villages under Parshivni tehsil being auctioned off, the sand mafia continues to conduct illegal sand excavation on a significant scale. Seven trucks, along with 10 brass sand and two Pokland machines, were confiscated by the police. The total worth of the seized vehicles and sand amounts to Rs 2 crore 20 lakh 20 thousand. A police operation was carried out at Waghoda Ghat on Kanhan river under Parshivni tehsil. Upon encountering the police presence, the individuals associated with the illegal activities at the ghat took advantage of the cover of night and fled the scene.

description:
Illegal sand lifting by influential construction agencies has been going on unabated in the blocks of Tirtol, Raghunathpur and Kujang in the district of Jagatsinghpur leading to severe erosion in the riverside villages. This is posing threat to the Taladanda and the Machhgaon canal embankment. Along with this alarming proportion of river erosion in the villages of these blocks stretched across the Mahanadi deltaic region, local land has been encroached illegally and on lease from farmers for stocking up mined river sand. Villagers alleged that local revenue officials are complicit with construction units and builders in carrying out illegal sand mining activities. This mining depletes the riverbed of sand, which is essential for retaining water and recharging the groundwater table. Without sand, water flows directly into the sea, exacerbating groundwater depletion and negatively impacting irrigation wells. The loss of sand and the subsequent decline in groundwater levels are predicted to cripple rain-fed agriculture, which is a primary source of livelihood for these rural communities. The long-term effect is expected to hinder the economic development of these areas.

Recently, a squad led by Tirtol tehsildar Ramesh Chandra Panda and the Inspector in Charge of Tirtol police station, Balaram Nayak, conducted a raid on sand lifting units on the Mahanadi riverbed. They seized eight heavy vehicles involved in illegal sand lifting and imposed a fine of ₹25,000 on each vehicle owner.

The BJP activists staged a road blockade, protesting against illegal sand mining, at Parjang in

Dhenkanal district saying that the administration has not been doing enough checks.

Later, a party delegation submitted a memorandum to the district collector, seeking closure of the sand quarries and immediate action against those involved in the unlawful activity in the area. The blockade was lifted after local Tehsildar reached the spot and promised the agitators of appropriate steps.

Illegal sand mining in the riverbeds of the Yamuna and Sindh rivers along the Uttar Pradesh-Madhya Pradesh border in the region is continuing in blatant violation of the Supreme Court's February 2012 ruling. Heavy-duty JCB machines were being used by contractors in the riverbed of the Yamuna and Sindh rivers for extracting sand in Etawah, Fatehpur and Jalaun districts. Villagers rue that despite the ban, on an average 50 to 100 trucks and tractor-trolleys carrying sand can be seen passing from the Fatehpur district.

Additional auctions for the remaining 25 ghats will be completed within 15-20 days, further increasing revenue. The third round of sand ghat auctions failed to attract any bids for the 18 ghats offered, prompting the government to reduce the offset price by 25%. The auction for 39 sand ghats in Nagpur district will be held on Tuesday, with excavation permitted until July 31, 2011. Initially, 96 ghats were identified, narrowed down to 62 by the Groundwater Survey and Development Agency (GSDA), and further reduced to 39 by gram sabhas.

Social worker Anil Agre and six others filed the petition, claiming that government officials were ignoring rampant illegal sand mining in various districts, including Nagpur, Bhandara, Gondia, Chandrapur, and Gadchiroli. They accused government and transport department officials of colluding with sand contractors, violating a 2013 policy that required environmental clearance and set conditions for sand mining. The petitioners argued that trucks often carried more sand than allowed, causing significant losses to the exchequer, and called for an expert inquiry into the matter.

State Home Minister Anil Deshmukh, along with Guardian Minister Nitin Raut, conducted surprise checks at sand ghats, seized vehicles, and visited police stations in the district. The home minister has issued instruction to use drones to monitor illgeal excavation and transportation of sand.

This case will be heard next on August 2, 2016.

The article speaks of the hurdles in the fight against illegal sand mining in the country focusing on the lacunas in the laws and policies surrounding minor minerals extraction especially sand. The article is from March 2015 preceding the new Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines issued in March 2016. 

The issue of sand mining had been known earlier as well, but gained significant legal prominence ever since the Supreme Court of India, in its order dated February 27, 2012, went on to systematically record how India’s rivers and its riparian ecology have been severely affected due to an “alarming rate of unrestricted sand mining.”  Recognising that small-scale mining of minor minerals from riverbeds is an important economic activity, the order noted that unrestricted and uncontrolled form of such mining has had a huge environmental impact.


Following this order, on August 5, 2013, the NGT's principal bench passed a strong order restraining the removal of minerals from riverbeds across the country without approvals by the Ministry of Environment and the concerned state-level environment impact assessment authorities. And also made strong observations regarding the non-compliance of its orders by state governments.

This large-scale extraction disrupts local ecosystems and impacts livelihoods dependent on the river, such as farming and fishing. The aggressive sand mafia, coupled with inadequate government response, exacerbates these issues. Birds and other wildlife that rely on the riverbanks are also affected. The overview shows that the sand mining state of affairs have further worsened in Andhra Pradesh. While the illegal and excessive riverbed mining continued to affect rivers, dependent communities & even aggravating the surface and groundwater crisis in Tungabhadra river villages in Kurnool and Palar tributaries in Chittoor. Mining in Varaha river and in the catchment of Kalyanapulova dam in Vishakhapatnam has been severely affecting tribal population and farmers by creating water scarcity.


The unsustainable mining practices in Nagavali, Krishna, Godavari and other rivers have not stopped. In fact, with new govt which made it an election issue and won has failed to reverse the trend. First it abruptly cancelled the existing policy and then delayed the much hyped new one for five months. The 15 days ban & then non-availability due to floods hit the construction sector severely rendering about 35 lakh sand and construction workers of which nearly 30 per cent were women- jobless. The crisis also reportedly led to suicide incidents of four labours.  


In between the govt could make available only 40,000 T sand a daily against the demand of about 1.50 lakh T. The online booking mechanism proved ineffective leading to shortage & exorbitant price rise in the black market thus creating a new mafia. With availability of 12 MCM sand against the demand of 20 MCM annually, APMDC officials say Andhra Pradesh is sand-deficit. Govt also says that due to illegal mining state was losing Rs 500-600 crore revenue annually. Criticising free sand policy the govt promised to avail sand at Rs 375 per T through APMDC but the non-availability led to about 10 times price rise in black market. 


In a face saving move, it allowed more mining in smaller rivers, village level water bodies and even explored more mining opportunities in already over-exploited rivers and Kadapa and Prakasam districts. However the policy changes have not helped stop unsustainable exaction and plug illicit mining operations. It is surprising that despite this riverbed minerals were being transported to Bengaluru, Chennai and Telangana while given short supply, the builders in state were seen buying sand from Odisha. Reports also show that the state govt has failed to install CCTV cameras and has not taken other measures recommended by MoEF&CC to check illegal sand mining. 


In an unexpected U-turn, the Jagan Mohan Reddy govt has denied illegal mining in Krishna river by submitting same affidavit which was presented by previous govt in NGT. The TDP govt had maintained that it allowed dredging and desliting which was out of EIA ambit. Thus the present govt has further betrayed the mandate and trust of people affected and concerned about the brazen mining operations.


The root cause of sand vortex in Andhra Pradesh is undoubtedly war footing construction work in nine cities including capital Amravati undertaken post bifurcation of state driving up the land prices and sand demand. The cities cannot be called smart if their construction is being done by unsustainable extraction of riverbed mineral which is essentially leading to destruction of rivers and water sources.


Talking of violence, five people including four govt officials and a village representative faced violent attacks for acting against illegal mining activities and four labours reportedly committed suicide following sand scarcity in the state.


The efforts by water activist Rajendra Singh, Vikram Soni, Anumolu Gandhi and Bolisetty Satyanarayana in exposing the illegalities in Krishna river sand mining are appreciable. However, the present govt has taken no lesson from the failure of previous govt and more or less marching on the same path when it comes to mining practices. In absence of scientific replenishment studies and EIA scrutiny the new sand mining policy has not helped the govt, rivers or people.
