description: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) directed the Andhra Pradesh government to take strict action against illegal sand mining by prosecuting violators, imposing penalties, and enforcing regulations. No act of sand mining in the guise of desilting or dredging is to be permitted in the river, reservoir, lakes and pond beds. It ordered the state to survey sediment deposits, follow environmental guidelines, and create monitoring mechanisms, including GPS for transport vehicles and CCTV at mining sites, to prevent unauthorized activities. The NGT also mandated the formation of a permanent Expert Appraisal Committee in each district to conduct environmental assessments and ensure sustainable sand mining practices.

Mining of sand in Tungabhadra river near Gundrevula in C Belagal mandal of Kurnool district has led to a row between people of border villages of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, which are already locked in a controversy over sharing Krishna river waters.

People of border villages levelled allegations against each other that sand was being illegally mined in their respective territory.

Andhra Pradesh’s strict crackdown on illegal sand mining, especially in the Rayalaseema region, has sharply reduced sand availability in Bengaluru, doubling local prices and halting some construction. The shortage stems from AP's successful prevention of unauthorized sand transport, previously a primary sand source for Karnataka. Neighboring states are now struggling to meet sand demands.

The article speaks of a report that mentions that unchecked sand mining in Karnataka's Malaprabha river basin significantly worsened flooding. Sand extraction depleted riverbeds, reducing their capacity to hold water and leading to increased flood damage. The resulting ecological imbalance disrupted local agriculture, groundwater levels, and increased sediment in the river. The report urges stringent regulation and restoration measures to address environmental and economic impacts caused by illegal sand mining.


It also mentions how government loses revenue when sand mining is illegally done.

The State Government is set to revive sand mining in rivers within the Kulathupuzha forest range after a decade of hesitation. The plan is to mine sand from Millpaalam and Chozhiyakodu banks, where there is an abundance of sand, for residential purposes. The initiative was suspended in 2009 due to complaints of diversion of sand meant for BPL families to civil contractors. The River Management Authority found mining feasible and desirable in the area. The project will involve 5,500 cubic meters of sand from each point, with the profit distributed among vana samrakshana samithis for both mining and transporting the sand.

A raid was conducted by the Mines and Minerals Department, on the lease of Narmada river passing near Fatehpur near Nareshwar in Karjan taluka and valuables worth Rs. 2.5 crore were seized. Despite the ban on mining in the river from 6 pm to 6 am, many leaseholders are engaged in unbridled sand mining even at night. To stop this mining, an investigation was conducted by the mining teams. Sources said that after the illegal sand mining, now penal action will be taken.

district: Chennai, Ariyalur, Karur, Thanjavur, Tiruchirappalli, Vellore
description:
Enforcement Directorate in its letter to the Tamil Nadu DGP alleged:


• Collusion between government officials and private excavator-owning contractors in a sand mining scam worth Rs 4,730 crore.

• The agency has pegged the illegally mined sand at 23.64 lakh units in the 2020-2023 period.

• Contractors illegally mined sand across vast areas adjacent to those leased for mining by the Public Works Department (PWD).

• Mining was carried out across 105 hectares, including areas adjacent to approved sites.

• The total lease area given to contractors was around 190 hectares across 28 sites in five districts, but the total area mined was estimated at 987 hectares.

• The agency has also substantiated excess mining by analysing GPS coordinates of 273 excavator machines sold by M/s Kobelco and JCB to 16 customers in the state.

• The agency has provisionally attached assets worth Rs 130 crore, including 209 sand excavators worth Rs 128.34 crore.

• Collectors of five districts appeared before the ED after they were summoned for questioning.

A two-judge panel of the Telangana High Court on Monday ordered notices to the managing director of Telangana State Mineral Development Corporation and others in a public interest litigation alleging illegal mining activities at Bichkunda, Kamareddy. The panel of Chief Justice Alok Aradhe and Justice J. Sreenivas Rao treated a letter addressed to the Chief Justice by the President Bar Association, Bichkunda mandal and others as PIL.


The letter states that illegal sand mining activities are taking place in Bichkunda mandal, more specifically in the Khadgam – Shetlur suburbs. The letter revealed that though deeply concerned, the local residents fear filing complaints due to intimidations and threats posed by people involved. It is stated that previous government had issued permissions for sand mining in six quarries in the Khadgam – Shetlur suburbs, whose validity had expired long back


It is alleged in the letter that according to regulations, the miners are supposed to deposit the excavated sand in designated areas for sale under Telangana State Mineral Development Corporation. Instead the sand miners, in collusion with officials, were illegally transporting sand to Maharashtra, Karnataka and other states.

The Congress party in Kerala is calling for an investigation into a recent government order related to sand mining. They allege that the order could lead to environmental harm and is aimed at benefiting certain private interests. The party has raised concerns about the legality and implications of the order, urging authorities to review its impact on the environment and local communities.

This report talks about the fact that illegal sand mining is widespread in Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh, with sand mafias exploiting relaxed regulations, particularly during election periods. Though nine sand reaches were officially designated for mining, authorities struggle to control over-extraction. A planned CCTV system to monitor sand mining was obstructed due to political influences, allowing unchecked sand extraction. The district collector has announced intentions to expand officially sanctioned mining sites and install surveillance in certain areas to address the problem.

On October 12, over 340 activists from the Cauvery Protection Movement were arrested in Karur district, Tamil Nadu, while protesting against illegal sand mining along a 3-km stretch of the Cauvery riverbed. They provided video evidence of the ongoing mining, which they claim has not been controlled, and demanded the closure of these operations, referencing a 2010 Madras High Court ruling that banned sand quarrying in another river. The activists highlighted the negative impact of excessive mining on groundwater levels and the ecosystem, as sand plays a crucial role in water percolation and table recharge. The movement also called for the Cauvery delta to be declared a protected agricultural zone to prevent industrial activities. An expert committee is set to report on sustainable sand mining practices to the Supreme Court, amid ongoing concerns about water depletion in the region due to both climate and mining activities.

Illegal sand mining has been taking place for over a year at the Cooum river mouth near Napier Bridge in Chennai, with lorries operating between midnight and 2 a.m., bypassing both Public Works Department (PWD) and police surveillance. The lorries enter a narrow lane adjacent to the Anna Square bus stand one at a time, guarded by two men, as reported by witnesses. Some lorries were even found to have registration numbers that matched motorbikes. 


PWD officials confirmed that no approvals had been granted to any government or private agency for such mining activities. S. Rama Prabhu, State Secretary of the Builders Association of India, highlighted the risks of using sea sand for construction, warning that it is unfit for building and will lead to poor-quality structures. S. Yuvaraj, President of the Tamil Nadu Sand Lorry Owners Federation, estimated that the sand is being sold for ₹40,000 to ₹50,000 per load. 


Visible pits, from which the sand was extracted, were observed by an Indian Express team. Experts raised concerns about the environmental impact, including damage to the coastal ecosystem and increased saline water intrusion into the area. When contacted, PWD engineers assured that immediate action would be taken.

The Indian government has confirmed widespread illegal sand mining along the Yamuna River in Noida, following a report from a three-member committee. The committee found violations of environmental laws and court orders, despite clear regulations. The issue gained attention after IAS officer Durga Shakti Nagpal was transferred, allegedly for her crackdown on illegal mining. The mining, estimated at ₹10 crores per day, has caused environmental damage, including the shifting of the Yamuna’s course by 500 meters. The government plans further action and recommends regular monitoring and disaster management measures due to the region’s seismic risks.

18 boats that were allegedly engaged in extracting sand across the Godavari river were seized by the water resource department of Andhra Pradesh. Sand mining here is posing a threat to the structural stability of the bridge in Rajahamendravaram.

A late- night raid conducted by the Industries and Mines Department resulted in the seizure of 125 vehicles, including Hitachi excavators, loaders, and dumpers, involved in the theft of mineral resources from the banks of Banas River. Sand worth 3.25 crore was seized.


It uncovered a large-scale operation siphoning off precious mineral resources from the riverbed. The seized vehicles, which included trucks of various sizes, were found to be carrying far more sand than their legal capacity. Many of these trucks were likely making multiple trips per day. The raid was initiated following complaints from local residents about the rampant illegal mining activities in the area.

Vadodara Mines and Minerals raided illegal sand mining in the Mahisagar riverbed of Poicha-Kanoda village. Illegal mining was busted at night in the Orsang River, which passes near Karnali and Piplia villages in Dabhoi taluka. 


Miners go inside the Mahisagar river bed up to 100 feet and dig sand and sell it, using  equipment like canoes, vacuum pumps, Hitachi machines, JCBs.


It is worth mentioning that recently, a flying squad from Gandhinagar raided the Mahi river, seizing sand worth 90 lakhs, they took action, even after that, illegal mining activities continued.

The Mines and Minerals Department conducted a raid on the illegal sand mining going on in the Mahi river passing through Khandi Jalampura area under Parthampura Gram Panchayat of Savli taluka, causing a stampede among the sand mafia. Sand mafia is illegally mining sand in the Mahi river passing through Savli taluka. 


Raids conducted by the flying squad and mining department of Vadodara, and sand worth 2.6 crores were seized including 2 machines, 2 loaders, 8 dumpers, and 9 tractors. Sources said that the names of two people who were involved in illegal sand mining in the Mahi River, Ankit Patel (Resident of Anjesar, Ta. Savli) and Arjun Singh Padhiyar (Resident of Jalampura, Ta. Savli), have been revealed.

The news report mentions about the impact of sand mining in Madauli Khurd village, Banda district, Uttar Pradesh. Farmers are living in terror on day-to-day basis because of the mining activities and terror of sand syndicate. Vegetables grown by them in their fields have been destroyed because of excess water flowing in their fields caused by sand mining.


Overloaded sand trucks continuously passing from their village is causing damage to the road, and causing accidents. Its a violation of law that sand miners are supposed to create an alternate path / road, which they have not done in this case. District authorities have imposed a fine in this illegal mining, but still mining has not stopped. mposing fines is not a soluton, rather a case should be registered to stop the illgal mining activitis. Farmers mention that the sand mining is taking place beyond the allotted lease land.

The Pradhan Nagar police in Siliguri arrested a man for illegally extracting and smuggling sand from the Mahananda River near Gulma. The investigation is ongoing and further action will be taken against those involved in the illegal mining and smuggling operation.

description: The West Bengal Mineral Development and Trading Corporation Limited (WBMDTCL) has recently issued a notification stating that sand can be extracted from 21 rivers of West Bengal, including Mayurakshi, Kangsabati, Ajay, Damodar, Tarakeswar, Silabati, Subarnarekha, Mahananda etc. Environmental activist Subhash Dutta has written a letter to the Chief Secretary of West Bengal and Principal Secretary of the Irrigation Department and the Chairman of the West Bengal Mineral Development and Trending Corporation, with a request to stop the extraction of sand from the rivers.

The National Green Tribunal’s (NGT) Eastern Zone Bench in Kolkata constituted a committee comprising experts from the Central Pollution Control Board, West Bengal Pollution Control Board, and the District Magistrate of Darjeeling to address the environmental issue of illegal mining of sand and stone from the Balason and Rakti rivers near Siliguri, West Bengal,  which has been allegedly damaging the Putinbarie tea estate’s roads and affecting tea production due to flooding from the rivers.

A surprise raid by the CM Flying Squad in Palwal district uncovered an illegal sand mining racket. The raid, led by DSP Rajdeep Mor, revealed a stockpile of 400 metric tonnes of illegally mined river sand at Sultanpur village, near the Yamuna River. The sand was found dumped at three locations without any official records or claimants, raising suspicions of unauthorized activity.


Revenue Department officials, including the local Patwari, have been directed to take action against the landowners where the sand was found. Inspector Jagdish led the team, which included officers from the Mining and Revenue Departments. The seized sand stock has prompted officials to pursue the registration of an FIR against the unidentified individuals involved in the illegal mining operation.

The article covers in detail the story of river Bagen which flows through Madhya Pradesh and meets Yamuna in Banda district of Uttar Pradesh. It explains how Bagen and Ken with their associated rivers and irrigation canals are the lifeline of the people of Bundelkhand. And, also gives detailed account of the several challenges which the locals had to face due to rampant sand mining on these rivers. The ecology of these rivers is in grave danger so is the future of the drought prone areas like Banda. The lack of accountability on the part of authorities and free hand which the sand mine operators enjoy makes life difficult for the local residents.

description: The article gives an overview of the dire state of the important rivers like Ken and Betwa. Sewage, industrial waste and rampant sand mining being the major threats to all the rivers like Narmada, Chambal, Shipra etc. In Madhya Pradesh, Chambal, Khan and Shipra were identified as the most polluted rivers. Additionally, the energy outputs of the two hydroelectric power projects on river Betwa is dwindling. Also, it talks about the looming threat of Ken-Betwa river interlinking project which could be the death knell for these rivers.

Sand smuggling near T-bridge on Mahanadi in Cuttack's Baideswar threatens its structure. Collector Dattatraya Shinde enforces Section 163, targets mafias involved in the illegal activity.


According to sources, several mafias are active in the region and are earning handsomely in the absence of regular raids by the local administration. Concrete pillars of the bridge are facing threats as the minor mineral is illegally being quarried from around the structure.

The district administration’s failure to check illegal sand lifting from Mahanadi and Devi river beds is not only leading to loss of revenue but also hampering construction activities in different areas of Jagatsinghpur. This has led to shortage of sand, which is used in construction activities, and as a result of which its price has skyrocketed.

Shaik Jalal, an 18 year old student of a local higher secondary school in Brahmabarada and Chandpur areas of Jajpur district, Odisha, was reported missing on Wednesday after he went to take bath in the Brahmani river along with his friend. Eye-witnesses stated that while bathing, his friend slipped into a deep water pit and Jalal dived in to save him. While Jalal successfully saved his friend, he himself went missing soon after. On Thursday morning his body was found floating at the bazaar ghat and fished out by rescue personnel.

description: The government revised the sand mining policy to introduce online sale of sand. Depots will be set up in all districts. A single tender will be invited for excavation, transport and construction. Monitoring will be done at tehsil level as per National Green Tribunal rulings. The cabinet also decided that the rate of sale should be on a no profit no loss basis. The sand mining policy was aimed at curbing the illegal extraction of sand especially from areas around river beds and its sale on the black market. A technical committee at tehsil level would monitor the riverbed for excavation while a committee headed by collector would oversee the tendering and sale.

The National Green Tribunal (NGT) July 16, 2024 directed constitution of a three member committee to look into the allegations of illegal sand mining in Mahanadi river at Chikhili in Ambavona tehsil, Bargarh district, Odisha. It was alleged that an illegal miner had extracted approximately 200,000 cubic metres of sand unlawfully.

The National Green Tribunal constituted a joint committee to probe into allegations of illegal extraction of sand allegedly by using excavators from Mahanadi river bed at Nuapatana under Tangi-Choudwar tehsil of Cuttack district. The committee shall examine the site and submit its report stating therein specifically as to whether excess sand has been excavated beyond the licence granted and  whether heavy machines have been used for excavation of sand which is contrary to the rules. The committee shall also enumerate  any violation of the environmental clearance certificate or consent to operate

National Green Tribunal issued fresh orders to the joint inspection committee to expand its probe to all the alleged sites in Bargarh and Jharsuguda districts where illegally extracted sand from the Mahanadi river is being stockpiled. 


The committee was formed by NGT to probe illegal mining of sand from the Mahanadi and hoarding in Bargarh and Jharsuguda districts on July 16. In the additional affidavit, the petitioner said the private lessee is continuing with illegal mining and dumping sand in various places. But the committee visited only one alleged site and ignored all the others where the private lessee is also dumping/stacking illegally extracted sand.

JD(S) leader from Bhadravati Ajit Gowda and his associates recorded videos of alleged illegal sand mining along the Bhadra river banks. The footage captured earthmover machines and tractors extracting sand from the riverbank.


They alerted the officials and upon arrival found the extracted sand abandoned and the perpetrators had fled. They plan to file an official complaint with the Lokayukta

Illegal sand mining from rivers such as Bagjan, Neora, and Shaulmari in Domohani village, located in the Maynaguri C.D. block of Jalpaiguri district, West Bengal, has caused significant environmental and infrastructural damage. Rampant extraction has led to the erosion of riverbanks, destruction of village roads, and harm to cultivated fields and tea gardens along the rivers. Residents who protested against the sand mafia have faced threats, and despite filing multiple complaints, authorities have failed to take concrete action to curb the issue.

A report by the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People reveals that at least 193 people died due to illegal sand mining in India between January 2019 and November 2020. The highest fatalities (95) occurred in North India, while South India reported the least. Most deaths (148) resulted from accidents, including drowning in deep sand pits (95), mine collapses (27), and road accidents involving sand-laden vehicles (26). Violence linked to illegal mining caused 45 deaths, including villagers, government officials, activists, and reporters. Minors and teenagers made up 80% of drowning victims. Additionally, 84 incidents of threats and attacks were reported against those opposing illegal mining. The actual numbers could be much higher due to underreporting.


Note - The news report is based on a report published by a civil society organisation. The report collated news reports from across India that have reported on deaths caused due to / around sand mining.

Three people died and three were injured after a sand mine caved in during illegal sand mining in Jabalpur district of Madhya Pradesh. The incident occurred while labourers were extracting sand from Barnu river for a temple construction in Katra Ramkhiria village, around 40km from Jabalpur. Among those killed were Munni Bai Basod, 50, her son Mukesh, 35, and labour contractor Rajkumar Khatik, 25.

Rural police in Ludhiana have booked three persons for loading sand in tractors allegedly brought from the riverbed of the Sutlej. The police said they got a tip-off about the activity when they were on patrolling duty at Krishanpura Chowk in Sidhwan Bet area. However, the accused escaped. Police seized the four tractors.

NGT criticized the Odisha government over its failure in curbing illegal smuggling of sand from the Mahanadi river bed. The green panel has also imposed a fine of Rs 38 lakh on the lease holders. The tribunal also directed the State government to take stringent measures to check illegal sand mining. the State government has been directed to install CCTV cameras at all the leased out sand mines along the Mahanadi river bed, ensure that the trucks engaged in transporting sand are fitted with GPS and take help of satellite pictures to zoom in on illegal lifting of sand.

Illegal sand miners attacked forest officials and fled with two tractor-trolleys loaded with sand that the team had seized in Madhya Pradesh's Chhatarpur district. The incident took place in the Bada Malhera area within the jurisdiction of Gulganj police station.


Forest Range Officer Rajendra Pastor said they had received information about illegal sand mining in a river under the Bhartoli forest beat. Acting on the input, forest officials from Bada Malhera and Gulganj went to the area and seized two tractor-trolleys from the spot. However, Shailendra Singh, a resident of Gadha, allegedly tried to run a tractor-trolley over the forest officials. He also damaged a forest department vehicle and then fled with the sand-laden vehicles along with other workers.

Sand mafias are daringly excavating and transporting sand illegally from the Chambal River in Barkheda village, Ratlam district, Madhya Pradesh, right past the Barkheda police station without any repercussions. Mining operations near the Joganiya Mata pilgrim site involve the use of JCBs to extract sand directly from the riverbed. Despite the illegal activities occurring openly, the Barkheda police have not taken any significant action. Mining department launched a raid on the mafias' hideouts. However, the mafias managed to escape with their vehicles before the team could apprehend them. Nevertheless, two tractors were seized during the raid. The audacity of these mafias and the lack of concrete action by the authorities have left locals frustrated and demanding urgent measures to address this blatant lawlessness.

A team of officials led by Birbhum district magistrate Bidhan Ray raided at least three illegal sand mines at midnight, a week after chief minister Mamata Banerjee had publicly rebuked him for the unauthorised extraction of sand from riverbeds. The raids were conducted after the officials received a tip-off that sand was mined illegally from the Ajay river in the Nanoor area after midnight and a larger part of the sand went to Jharkhand.

Allegations of illegal sand smuggling have emerged from various areas in Jalpaiguri, including the Karala River near Jalpaiguri Sadar Block Assam More. Acting on reports of lack of royalties, the Rajganj Block Land and Land Reforms Department conducted a raid, seizing four sand-laden dumpers and imposing a fine of Rs. 45,000 on each. However, tensions flared during the penalty process as dumper owners confronted the Land Revenue Department staff. The owners argued that there was no standardized rate for royalty payments, and when charged, the rates were excessively high. They warned that if a fixed pricing system is not established for future royalty payments, a section of them may resort to protests and even suicide.

Illegal sand mining in the Nagavali River within the Amudalavalasa Assembly constituency of Srikakulam is causing severe environmental damage and public safety risks. The sand mafia, allegedly supported by officials and political leaders, operates earth movers round-the-clock, extracting sand without concern for environmental impact or the river’s fate.


Despite National Green Tribunal (NGT) guidelines issued in 2010 to regulate mining activities in water bodies, officials from mines, geology, and revenue departments have failed to enforce restrictions. Experts and retired irrigation officials warn that rampant mining could alter the river’s course, weaken bundhs, and threaten drinking water and irrigation projects in the district. Meanwhile, the unchecked operations are also damaging roads and causing traffic issues, raising concerns about public safety.

Goa Coastal Zone Management Authority (GCZMA), after inspection, found evidence of illegal sand mining at Chorao and Vanxim island, and its surrounding areas. Locals of Devguim wado and Chamerem wado had complained of illegal sand extraction from the Mandovi river, and alleged that mangroves have been destroyed and a mud road has been built.

Accordingly, the GCZMA carried out an inspection of the area and found that mud filling has been done to build a mud road leading to the river. The property lies within the no-development zone of the river with mangroves, which is classified as a CRZ-III area.

A violent clash erupted in Birbhum’s Kankartala area over control of illegal sand mining operations in the Ajay river, allegedly involving rival factions backed by Trinamool Congress (TMC). Crude bombs were thrown during the fight, resulting in serious injuries to a man named Sheikh Saktar Ali, whose right leg was amputated. Another person was also injured. Ten people has been arrested by police.


Residents have long accused local TMC-backed groups of illegal sand extraction. The incident follows Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee’s recent reprimand of district officials over sand smuggling. BJP leader Anup Saha blamed factions linked to Anubrata Mondal and Sheikh Kajal for the violence. Mondal, recently released on bail in a cattle smuggling case, is reportedly at odds with Kajal. The TMC has denied any involvement, stating the clash was a local dispute and that police will take necessary action.

Police and mining officials busted an illegal mining gang in Jhugian Peer Bakhash village near the Sutlej river on Tuesday night. They seized a poclain machine and four tipper trucks from outside the designated mining area. Villagers complained that illegal mining damaged roads and disrupted their lives. A case has been registered under relevant laws, but the local SHO did not respond to calls or messages.

Three boats seized in raids by Vadodara Rural Municipality and police on illegal sand mining activities from Mahi River. A dumper and a quantity of sand of about one hundred tons were also found. Which has been handed over to the Mines and Minerals Department. The value of all this is approximately Rs. Five lakhs.

Due to indiscriminate sand mining without government control, the banks and ravines in the Narmada coastal area have been severely eroded. The government is silent against the sand mafia and due to this, the ravine collapsed last September and most of the area of ​​the Bakul Ashram, including the temple with the revered idols, was submerged in the river. Due to the government's inaction, the ashram has suffered a loss of approximately 12 lakhs.


On September 19, 2024, A loud crashing sound started coming from the temple, and within an hour, the children's garden in the ashram, which contained sports equipment, a 5,000-liter drinking water tank with a motor, the idols enshrined in the temple, a 7.7 kg floating rock proving the authenticity of the Ramayana, and other things of religious importance, all were submerged in the waters of the Narmada. 


Sand mining has been going on on a large scale from the river bank opposite Bakul Ashram for the last two to three years by the so-called lease holders and is still going on. In addition, due to the unplanned release of large amounts of water from the Narmada Dam, the soil layers of the ravines on the banks of the Narmada have become eroded and hollow, which is why hundreds of temples and ashrams on the banks of the Narmada, like Bakul Ashram, are under threat.

The Land Reforms Department, with the assistance of the Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB), conducted a joint operation in Panitanki, Siliguri, near the Nepal border, to curb illegal sand mining and smuggling. On the first day of the operation, 16 tractors loaded with illegally mined sand were seized, as confirmed by Pratima Subba, the Land Reforms Officer of Kharibari Block. She stated that local complaints prompted the raid, and since none of the seized vehicles had valid permits, legal action has been initiated. Future raids are planned if further complaints arise.


The Mechi River, which forms the border between India and Nepal at Panitanki, has long been a hotspot for illegal sand mining. Allegations suggest that sand smuggling occurs at night using trucks and dumpers, disturbing local residents with noise. Despite multiple complaints, previous police and administrative actions were ineffective. There are also accusations of involvement by certain Trinamool leaders, police personnel, and administrative officials in facilitating the smuggling.


Due to legal complexities, police face challenges in conducting raids near the border, which has led to an increase in unauthorized sand transportation. The illegal mining has reportedly deepened the Mechi River, causing it to shift further into Indian territory. Following the recent joint operation by the Land Reforms Department and SSB, mining activities have temporarily ceased, with police also providing support.


While a leased sand mining site exists near Mechi, most extractions occur beyond the designated area without proper permits, leading to tax evasion and inflated prices for sand and stone. The surge in house construction work under government scheme has further exacerbated the issue, affecting consumers.

Despite a ban on using machines and sieves for sand extraction in the Damodar River, a private company has been illegally extracting sand using pipes and sieves. This activity has been reported along the border of Purba Bardhaman and Bankura districts. Vivek Dattatreya Bhasme, Additional District Magistrate (Land and Land Reforms, Bankura), confirmed that an investigation has been initiated.


The company is accused of digging 30-40 feet deep pits in the riverbed near the Tasuli area of Patrasayer Block in Bankura district, adjacent to Shillya in Galsi 1 Block, Purba Bardhaman. The extracted sand is then filtered and transported to Kolkata and other cities in the state. Authorities fear this illegal mining could lower the groundwater level, dry up tube wells, disrupt drinking water supply, and even alter the river’s course.


The Mines and Minerals Corporation recently imposed a ban on using sieves and machinery for sand extraction in the Damodar. However, the company continues its operations openly. The Galsi 1 Block administration claims that although sand-laden trucks pass through their area, the extraction takes place in Bankura’s Patrasayer Block, making it beyond their jurisdiction. Even when trucks are stopped, they present valid documents, preventing legal action.


Officials suspect that the company is exploiting the fact that the disputed area lies on the border between two districts. Patrasayer’s Block Land and Land Reforms Officer (BLLRO), Pradip Mondal, stated that he was unwell and busy with election duties but will now look into the matter.

The Subdivisional Magistrate (SDM) of Mandi was attacked by members of a mining mafia near Mandi town, Himachal Pradesh. 


The SDM was inspecting illegal sand mining along the Beas river when he was assaulted by three individuals, resulting in a broken tooth. He was alone, without police protection, and was taken to a government hospital by his driver. One attacker has been arrested and the search is ongoing for the others.


Despite a ban, illegal sand mining remains rampant in the Beas river stretch between Pandoh and Mandi.

Residents of Chibinang in West Garo Hills (WGH) are facing severe riverbank erosion along the Rongai River, attributed to an iron barricade placed decades ago and uncontrolled illegal sand mining. The barricade, installed near the envisioned Rongai Valley project dam site, disrupts the river's natural flow, increasing pressure on the banks and leading to substantial land loss. Despite repeated appeals to government agencies, no effective intervention has been made. Local residents have called for the immediate removal of the barricade and the construction of embankments to prevent further erosion. A previous embankment project was sanctioned but proved inadequate due to annual monsoon floods. Residents have also criticized the government's lack of support and raised concerns over unchecked illegal sand mining, which is exacerbating the situation. They urge authorities to take urgent action to protect the riverbanks, safeguard homes, and prevent an impending disaster.

district: Jamui, Nawada, Rohtas, Aurangabad, Patna, Saran, Vaishali, Kaimur (Bhabua)
description: Bihar police have launched a major crackdown on illegal sand mining, arresting 20 sand smugglers and seizing 40 boats in Patna’s Bihta region along the Sone River. During the raid, some smugglers set fire to around 10 boats to create a diversion. Despite previous police action, illegal mining operations persist, often backed by powerful mafias that operate across multiple districts. These criminal networks are well-armed and have repeatedly attacked police officials, even killing officers in recent months. Reports suggest they receive political and administrative support, making enforcement challenging. In response, the Bihar government has announced plans to establish permanent check posts in key districts to combat the growing illegal sand trade.

The Yamuna River is facing severe ecological degradation due to excessive sand mining, especially in its upstream stretch in Yamunanagar, Haryana. Locals report a drastic decline in bird and fish populations, disturbed habitats, and falling groundwater levels, all caused by the relentless extraction of sand. This has disrupted traditional livelihoods like fishing, farming, and boating, forcing communities into labour jobs and causing health and environmental issues.


Despite a 2012 Supreme Court ruling highlighting the dangers of sand mining to river ecosystems, little has been done to protect the Yamuna. Experts warn that the river’s biodiversity is being irreversibly damaged, yet no scientific studies have specifically examined the impact on Yamuna’s ecology. Villagers feel abandoned by authorities, who they say have prioritised profits from mining over the well-being of both the river and the people who depend on it.

district: Banda, Agra, Aligarh, Allahabad, Ambedkar Nagar, Azamgarh, Baghpat, Bahraich, Ballia, Auraiya, Balrampur, Bara Banki, Bareilly, Basti, Bijnor, Budaun, Bulandshahr, Chandauli, Chitrakoot, Deoria, Etah, Etawah, Faizabad, Farrukhabad, Fatehpur, Firozabad, Gautam Buddha Nagar, Ghaziabad, Gorakhpur, Hamirpur, Hardoi, Hathras (Mahamaya Nagar), Gonda, Jalaun, Jaunpur, Jhansi, Ghazipur, Jyotiba Phule Nagar, Kannauj, Kanpur Dehat, Kushinagar, Kheri, Lucknow, Mahrajganj, Lalitpur, Mahoba, Mainpuri, Mathura, Mau, Kaushambi, Meerut, Mirzapur, Moradabad, Muzaffarnagar, Kanshiram Nagar, Pilibhit, Pratapgarh, Rae Bareli, Kanpur Nagar, Rampur, Saharanpur, Sant Kabir Nagar, Shrawasti, Siddharthnagar, Sitapur, Sonbhadra, Shahjahanpur, Sultanpur, Unnao, Varanasi, Sant Ravidas Nagar (Bhadohi), Shamli
description: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) ordered Uttar Pradesh to halt all sand mining operations until replenishment studies were conducted, ensuring sustainable extraction. This directive, issued on May 6, 2022, followed complaints about illegal mining in Kanwara and Bendakhadar villages (Banda district), which violated the Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines (SSMMG), 2016, and Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining (EMGSM), 2020. The tribunal stressed that sand mining should only proceed after scientific studies confirm natural replenishment, preventing environmental degradation. The Central Mine Planning and Design Institute (CMPDI) was assigned to conduct these studies in Banda, while the Uttar Pradesh Pollution Control Board (UPPCB) was directed to ensure regulatory compliance.

The news report highlights an attempted attack on IAS officer Ram Mohan Meena by the sand mining mafia in Moradabad district, Uttar Pradesh, near the Dhela River on September 22. Meena and his team were trying to stop illegal mining when perpetrators attempted to run him over with tractors, but they fled after getting stuck in a sugarcane field. Following the incident, an FIR was filed against eight individuals, leading to the arrest of three suspects.The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has issued notices to the MoEFCC, district magistrates of Udham Singh Nagar (Uttarakhand) and Moradabad (Uttar Pradesh), as well as the pollution control boards of both states and the Centre. The NGT acknowledged that illegal sand mining is a long-standing issue, with culprits crossing state borders to evade law enforcement. The case is scheduled for hearing on January 22, 2025.

river: Betwa, Ken, Yamuna, Sone, Kathajodi, Narmada, Hooghly
description:
In India, sand mining surged after economic liberalization in the 1990s, becoming a large and frequently illegal industry. Despite existing regulations, weak enforcement has led to continued riverbed degradation. 

Sand mining across various Indian states is causing severe ecological damage, disrupting river flows, threatening infrastructure, and violating environmental regulations. In Uttar Pradesh's Ken River, mining over a 5-km stretch leads to pollution and ecological imbalance. Bihar's Son River faces structural risks due to excavation near bridges and railway tracks, while Haryana's Yamuna River sees violations of buffer zone regulations. Odisha's Kathajodi River experiences excessive mining near major bridges, with vague state laws offering little protection. Despite Madhya Pradesh's ban on mechanized mining, illegal operations continue along the Narmada. In West Bengal, suction pumps used in Hooghly River mining release toxins, endangering aquatic life. Weak enforcement and legal loopholes contribute to the unchecked exploitation of these rivers, necessitating stricter monitoring and compliance measures.

A new study highlights that restricting sand mining can help the critically endangered Yangtze finless porpoise population recover. Research in China's Dongting Lake, linked to the Yangtze River, found that mining activity had fragmented the porpoise habitat, increasing stress and reproductive challenges. By 2009, porpoise gaps in the lake reached 27 km, over a third of their range. Mining boats blocked migration routes and prevented prey fish from entering the lake. However, after a 2017 mining ban, porpoises returned to previously abandoned areas. With China cracking down on illegal sand mining, scientists are hopeful for the species' revival.

The Supreme Court, on November 10, 2021, allowed Bihar to continue mining activities through the Bihar State Mining Corporation, provided there is no environmental damage. The court highlighted that banning mining leads to illegal extraction, clashes between sand mafias, and loss of lives. It also stressed the importance of legal mining for public infrastructure and revenue generation.


The SC directed Bihar to prepare fresh District Survey Reports (DSRs) for mining in all districts, involving committees comprising officials from various departments. The draft DSRs must be completed within six weeks, followed by sequential approvals from the State Level Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC) and the State Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA), each within six weeks. The entire process must adhere to the 2020 Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining.


This order followed Bihar’s appeal against a National Green Tribunal (NGT) ruling that halted mining without SEAC and SEIAA approval. Bihar argued the NGT erred in its decision, causing revenue losses as old lessees continued mining for minimal fees. The SC permitted interim mining until DSRs are finalised.

The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has taken suo motu cognizance of a report on illegal sand mining in the Yamuna River floodplain between Alipur (North Delhi) and Panchayara (Ghaziabad). The tribunal, led by Justice Prakash Shrivastava, has sought responses from authorities, including district magistrates and pollution control boards. The report highlights unauthorized makeshift roads built with wooden planks and sandbags to transport mining equipment, causing environmental damage. The NGT noted that this violates the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act and raises concerns about large-scale encroachment by the sand mafia.

state: Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh
description:
Illegal riverbed mining in the Yamuna River at Vikas Nagar, Dehradun (Uttarakhand) has caused severe environmental damage. Miners have built a temporary bridge, used heavy machinery, and altered the river’s flow, violating mining regulations that prohibit obstructing river channels, using heavy machines, and mining near bridges and irrigation structures. The Haripur Bridge (connecting Vikas Nagar to Kalsi) is only 300 meters from the mining site, despite rules mandating a 500-meter safety buffer.


Locals fear flooding and land erosion and have protested against the mining, which is falsely labeled as flood protection work. Even during lockdowns, mining has continued 24/7. Two Himachal Pradesh forest guards were attacked near Paonta Sahib for opposing illegal mining, with the attackers later escaping to Vikas Nagar.


Illegal mining also threatens key infrastructure, including Shakti Canal and Dakpathar Barrage. Further upstream, at Bausan village (5 km away), a stone crusher unit has been mining riverbeds between Hathiyari and Katapathar, creating deep pits and causing air and noise pollution, harming local livelihoods. Another crusher unit at the Lakhwar Dam site conducted in-stream deep mining for a year without permission. Protests against it led to police harassment of villagers due to political involvement.


Illegal sand mining continues across the upper Yamuna segment in Haryana and Uttar Pradesh, despite frequent protests by villagers.

district: Agra, Bhind, Bundi, Dhaulpur, Etawah, Karauli, Kota, Morena, Sawai Madhopur, Sheopur
description: The Morena administration in Madhya Pradesh on Thursday banned sand mining as well as transportation from the Chambal River and also barred sale of fuel to unregistered vehicles to curb illegal activities and crime in the district.

Unabated illegal sand mining is posing a threat to the under-construction bridge on the Nagavali river as apprehensions are rife that the excess excavation from the nearby ramp will be a blow to the strength of the upcoming structure that will ensure connectivity between old and new Srikakulam. 


Recently, the government has opened a sand ramp in Hayatnagar, near where the new bridge is coming up, and it has proved a gold mine for sand transporters. The locals of Hayatnagar recently took to the streets alleging that sand is being transported illegally for the reach by lorries and tractors in the night to which officials have been turning a blind eye. Leading the protest, YSRC leader Dharmana Prasada Rao demanded a thorough probe into the allegations and necessary steps for the protection of new bridge. Illegal mining continues unabated from near the bridge in violation of the Water, Land Tree Act-2002 which says that sand excavation must not be undertaken near the bridge as it would lead to the collapse of the structure owing to lack of strength

Residents strongly resisted illegal  sand mining at Muddadapeta ramp in Nagavali river in Amadalavalasa Assembly constituency. The locals raised the issue in social media and it has attracted the attention of the State-level officials. Four persons who are residents of Munagavalasa, Kanugulavalasa, Amadalavalasa and Korlakota in Amadalavalasa Assembly constituency who are followers of a people’s representative formed into a group and excavated sand indiscriminately round-the-clock. 


Residents of Muddadapeta and its surrounding villages were worried over in-depth mining of sand in the river as it poses threat to river course and safety of its bunds. Following pressure from locals, Srikakulam revenue divisional officer (RDO), assistant director for mines and geology department and Amadalavalasa circle police rushed to spot and warned the mining mafia not to excavate sand. As a result, sand mining was stopped on Wednesdsay and also movement of lorries was not witnessed on the road.

The Kendrapara administration seized 19 trucks and two poclain excavators involved in illegal sand mining on the Chitrotpola riverbed at Bichana village under Garadapur tehsil. Acting on a tip-off, officials raided the site and confiscated the vehicles, which were transporting sand without obtaining any transit passes from the authorities. The drivers fled during the raid. However, fines will be imposed on the vehicle owners.


Residents of Bichana complained that heavy sand-laden vehicles have severely damaged village roads, which were last repaired two years ago. They also alleged that illegal sand mining is rampant due to high demand for construction materials, with local goons and contractors engaging in unchecked extraction. Additionally, clashes between rival sand mafia groups have worsened the law and order situation in the area.

The Jhelum River in Baramulla is facing a severe environmental crisis due to rampant illegal sand mining, particularly in Jahama, where excessive extraction has deeply altered the riverbed and disrupted its natural flow. The ongoing mining has lowered water levels, accelerated riverbank erosion, and increased the risk of severe flooding, threatening nearby infrastructure and settlements. Mushtaq Ahmad, an environmentalist warn that excessive sand removal destabilizes the riverbanks, making them vulnerable to flash floods. The destruction of the riverbed has also severely impacted the local ecosystem, disrupting fish breeding and endangering livelihoods dependent on the river.


Additionally, Ghulam Rasool, a retired teacher of the area said that unregulated sand extraction has also given rise to the criminal activities in the area. He said the lack of regulation has created a parallel black market for sand. The illegal trade has introduced easy, quick money into the hands of many youths, leading to an increase in substance abuse and drug addiction. Locals urge immediate government intervention to prevent irreversible environmental and social damage, warning that continued inaction could lead to an ecological disaster with long-term consequences for both nature and society.

The administration in Sehore has intensified its crackdown on illegal sand mining along the Narmada River. Bhairunda SDM Madan Singh Raghuvanshi, along with other officials, conducted surprise raids at Satdev, Tigali, Chhipaner, and other ghats, leading to the seizure of two JCB machines and over 12 tractor-trolleys. The sudden operation caused panic among the sand mafia, who fled, abandoning their vehicles, which were later taken to Bhairunda police station.


Despite efforts by the Mineral and Revenue Departments, including check posts and patrols, illegal sand mining continues unabated, significantly damaging the Narmada ecosystem and causing huge financial losses to the government. Many ghats, including Chhipaner, Tigali, and Satdev, lack authorized sand mines, yet large-scale illegal excavation persists.


SDM Raghuvanshi affirmed that strict actions will continue to curb illegal sand mining and ensure compliance with environmental and revenue regulations.

Authorities in Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh have informed the National Green Tribunal (NGT) about their actions against illegal sand mining after an attack on a joint magistrate near the Uttarakhand-UP border on September 22.


The Uttarakhand Pollution Control Board called for surveillance posts along the Kosi River and reported 82 impounded vehicles in six months. Officials confirmed ongoing illegal mining in Bajpur, Sultanpur, Mukandpur (Uttarakhand), and Pattikala Ghosipur (Uttar Pradesh).


The district magistrates of Udham Singh Nagar and Moradabad also detailed steps to stop illegal mining. The joint magistrate was attacked during an anti-encroachment operation when miners tried to run him over. Police later seized two tractor-trolleys and earthmovers from the site.

llegal sand mining has dried up the Gomti River in Katyur Valley, Kumaon (Bageshwar district, Uttarakhand), leaving villages without drinking water, especially during summer. Locals blame mining under the pretext of river dredging, which has reduced the river to a mere trickle. Despite repeated complaints, no effective action has been taken.


On Saturday, women from affected villages protested, blocking mining operations by sitting in front of dumpers and demanding an immediate halt. In response, the tehsildar visited the site and admitted that mining has polluted the river.


A Uttarakhand High Court advocate condemned the administration and mining operators, stating that negligence and illegal activities have caused the river to dry up.

The article reports that over the past 14 months, authorities in the Yamuna river region—particularly in Palwal and Faridabad—have registered 217 FIRs related to illegal sand mining. As a result of a special drive against the activity, police impounded around 188 vehicles and imposed penalties totalling approximately Rs 97.6 lakh. Despite these actions, the illegal mining continues, often occurring at night to meet high construction demand and fueled by alleged weak surveillance systems. The report also notes that the mining mafia has occasionally resorted to violence against officials, with incidents including an assault on a team trying to impound a vehicle and attacks on enforcement personnel. Officials have been urged to maintain strict vigilance, and the public is encouraged to report suspicious activities via a toll-free number.

To empower local tribal communities, the mining department initiated the process for allocating sand mining leases to residents of Scheduled Tribe areas in Sirohi. Under the new initiative, six leases will be granted across 14 revenue villages in two tehsils of the district. Officials from the mining department emphasised that the leases will not only benefit local individuals but also generate royalties for the department. The decision to grant local mining leases stems from a 2017 amendment to the mining department's rules. This initiative is part of a larger effort by the state govt to connect tribal communities with self-employment opportunities.

The Kulsi River in Kamrup, Assam, a vital habitat for the endangered freshwater river dolphin, is facing severe ecological distress due to extensive illegal mechanized sand mining. Local residents report that years of unregulated mining, particularly in the Chhaygaon branch of the river, have significantly lowered water levels, leading to habitat degradation for the dolphins.


Authorities have taken enforcement measures, with the Kamrup West Forest Division seizing and dismantling 49 suction machines between September and February. The region has one officially sanctioned sand extraction site under the Kulsi Forest Range, where only manual mining is permitted over a 4.95-hectare area for a seven-year period (2022-2029). Concerned citizens and environmental activists have strongly opposed mechanized sand mining.

Officials from the department of mines and geology faced a violent attack by illegal sand miners near Chikkasindogi village. This incident occurred when three officials raided an illegal sand mining site at Hirehalla.

During their attempt to halt the unlawful activities, eight sand smugglers present at the location became aggressive and assaulted one of the officials. Despite filing a complaint at the Alawandi police station, department sources indicated that the police are hesitant to register the complaint, as the accused are connected to an influential person, who has close ties with a local politician.

Illegal sand mining has been reported in Deroli Ahir village, located in Narnaul district, Haryana, following an inspection by the Mining and Geology Department. The illegal extraction of sand from the dried-up Dohan riverbed has reportedly been ongoing for several months, with local villagers involved in the activity. They have been using tractor-trailers to transport and sell sand at cheaper rates in nearby areas. Lakhi Ram Yadav, the Sarpanch of Deroli Ahir, who initially filed the complaint, mentioned that trees in the riverbed were also cut and sold by those engaged in the mining. Despite efforts to stop them, the perpetrators refused to comply and threatened the local leadership, prompting the Sarpanch to approach the authorities.


Mining Inspector Tanu Joshi confirmed that although no one was caught during the inspection, evidence of illegal sand mining was found. As a result, an inspection report and the Sarpanch’s complaint have been forwarded to the Haryana State Enforcement Bureau Police for legal action under the Mines and Minerals (Regulations and Development) Act, 1957.


The report also highlights that despite a district-wide ban on riverbed sand mining, similar illegal activities were reported in Nangal Choudhary area in April 2023, with sand often transported at night to avoid detection.

Second Part of a series report. Illegal sand mining in Kanalsi village, Haryana, is widespread and exceeds legal limits, harming farmland and the Yamuna river. Authorities are aware but take no action, and villagers’ complaints are ignored. Sand is heavily used in construction but is still treated as a ‘minor mineral,’ leading to weak rules. Experts warn this is damaging rivers, but enforcement is poor, and no research has been done on the impact.


Unlike the Ganga, which is protected under a national clean-up mission with strict controls, the Yamuna is left unprotected. India has research institutes for forests, but none for rivers, showing how little attention river health gets.

The Forest Department in Morena seized a truck carrying illegally mined sand from the Chambal River late at night on March 27, 2025. The driver alleged that the vehicle was destined for the Mungawali plant of Banku Kansana, son of Madhya Pradesh Agriculture Minister Aidal Singh Kansana. He claimed to have been transporting sand to the minister's son's plant for over eight days, earning ₹1,000 per day. The dumper, bearing "A Kansana" on its body, allegedly belongs to the minister's son. The driver also stated that multiple trucks and dumpers were involved in similar illegal mining activities, with the sand being used for road construction. A forest department SDO confirmed that the owner of the dumper was being identified and that the driver named the minister's son as the owner. In response, Minister Kansana denied ownership of the dumper, suggesting that political adversaries were attempting to tarnish his image.

​Illegal sand mining continues unabated along the Yamuna River's floodplains in Delhi, particularly in areas like Sonia Vihar and Jagatpur, despite clear prohibitions from the Supreme Court, Delhi High Court, and the National Green Tribunal (NGT). Nearly 200 trolleys and 50 dumpers of sand are illicitly extracted daily, causing significant environmental degradation to the riverbanks and ecosystem.


Environmental activist Varun Gulati has raised alarms about this ongoing exploitation, and alleges a nexus between the sand mafia and certain authorities, facilitated by substantial bribes. Despite these allegations, Delhi Police officials have denied the existence of illegal sand mining activities in the city. Town planner Pushkar Pawar warns that excessive sand extraction leads to riverbank erosion, loss of land and habitats, and water quality degradation. It disrupts aquatic ecosystems, diminishes groundwater recharge, and worsens water scarcity. Pawar advocates for stricter enforcement, including satellite and drone surveillance, public auctions for sand mining permits, and community participation in monitoring.


Despite no official sand mining permits in Delhi, illegal extraction persists in areas like Palla, Burari, and Sonia Vihar, with alleged complicity of local authorities.

Karnataka Government has granted permission to mine sand in 20 designated sand blocks in Udupi District. A total of 40,895 metric tonnes of sand can be mined from these sand blocks.


Mining has been approved in the following locations: Chaksomati Halla in Korangrapadi, Papanashini River and Chaksomati Halla in Manipura, Mogaveera Pete Salu Halla in Pejamangoor, Kudi Salu Halla in Kudi, four locations in Shiriyar Halla, two locations in Yadtadi Halla, Kavadi in Vaddarse, two locations in Hermunde Halla, Bollu Halla in Marne, Hoige Salu in Uloor, Shanadi Halla in Kedoor, Hirehole in Belur, Kubjahole in Kavradi, and Papanashini River in Kurkal.

This report by the Free Press Journal contains video recordings of an official of National Chambal Sanctuary purportedly discussing allowance of illegal sand mining on the river Chambal in exchange of bribes. In one of the videos, the official is recorded speaking about distribution of bribe money to other members of the system.

On the complaint of Sonipat Resident Pradeep Dahiya, the NGT has formed a joint panel to investigate the ground reality of destruction of flow of the Yamuna, because of illegal Sand Mining on the border of Haryana and Uttar Pradesh in Karnal district. The panel has been asked to submit its report within eight weeks and the NGT has fixed 31st July as the date of the next hearing. 


This seems to be a follow up of an existing case, as part of which a committee has already conducted on ground investigations, and submitted that a total area of 7414 square metres within the river's course had been mined upto a depth of 2 metres.

In Indore, illegal parking of sand-filled dumpers by traders on Nemawar Road is causing major traffic disruptions and posing accident risks. Despite repeated warnings, traders continue to encroach on public roads. Following persistent complaints from residents, Bicholi Hapsi SDM Roshni Vardhman and Tehsildar Ankita Vajpayee conducted an early morning raid and seized 10 illegally parked dumpers. Six were moved to a trenching ground, two to the police station, and two unfit dumpers were left on-site with notices. Similar issues persist on Dhar Road, where dumpers parked on main roads are worsening traffic conditions and posing accident risks, especially at night.

Despite ongoing efforts by the police and forest department, illegal sand mining continues in the prohibited area of National Chambal Gharial Sanctuary, Madhya Pradesh. In a recent operation, authorities seized a truck transporting sand from the sanctuary late at night. During interrogation, the truck driver alleged the vehicle belonged to "Banku Bhaiya," identified as the son of state Agriculture Minister Aidal Singh Kansana.


The driver claimed that sand is transported during nighttime, with drivers receiving ₹1,000 per trip. A video of the driver's statement has surfaced, further fueling the controversy. Congress state president Jitendra (Jitu) Patwari shared the video and accused the minister of being involved in “sand farming”. He criticized the BJP government, alleging widespread corruption among its ministers.

The havoc of the sand mafias excavating sand from the Chambal river continues in Morena, Madhya Pradesh. A youth named Sonu Goswami was seriously injured after being hit by a sand-laden tractor-trolley near Chachiha village in the Baghchini police station area. Villagers managed to stop the tractor near Bilgaon, after which the driver abandoned the vehicle and escaped. Police and forest department officials later seized the tractor. Sonu was initially taken to the district hospital and then referred to Gwalior in critical condition.

People stage a protest demanding controlling sand mining and focusing on fixing the roads being  used by trucks that transport sand. The poor road condition is impacting farmers and people from accessing roads, fields and cemetary. They are calling for the officials to look into the matter.

district: Amritsar, Barnala, Bathinda, Faridkot, Gurdaspur, Hoshiarpur, Muktsar, Patiala, Rupnagar, Sahibzada Ajit Singh Nagar, Sangrur, Shahid Bhagat Singh Nagar (Nawanshahr), Tarn Taran, Fatehgarh Sahib, Firozpur, Jalandhar, Kapurthala, Ludhiana, Moga, Mansa, Pathankot, Fazilka
description:
The Punjab Minor Minerals Policy was amended by a Council of Ministers during a Cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann.


Official claim: "legal supply of sand and gravel in Punjab represented only 4 per cent of the total available material (while the rest 96 per cent minerals are illegally mined or brought from outside the state), forms the basis of the amendments to the mining policy"


Major amendment points:


1. Individuals and crushers can now mine the minor minerals (sand and gravel) on the land owned by them by paying a royalty to the Punjab Government. 

2. The Cabinet also approved another amendment to the policy that allows government land to be cleared of sand on a “mission mode” with Deputy Commissioners authorised to grant NOCs for it.

बाँदा थाना मटौंध क्षेत्र के ग्राम मरौली खंड 5 मे बीते रविवार (April 20) को चट-चटगन निवासी रमैया किसान की 7 वर्षीय बेटी मौरम खदान के गड्ढे मे डूब गई है। जानकारी मुताबिक बेटी खेलते वक्त उक्त पानी भरे बड़े गड्ढे मे गिरी जिससे उसकी मौत हो गई। आनन फानन मे परिजनों ने जिला अस्पताल दिखाया लेकिन तब तक डाक्टर ने मृत घोषित कर दिया।


On 20th April, a 7 year old girl by the name Khushboo, drowned in a sand mining pit in Village Chak-Chatgan under the jurisdiction of Mataundh Police station in the Banda region. According to sources, while kids were playing, Khushboo fell into a mining pit that was full of water. By the time the child was taken to the hospital, it was already too late.

The article shares details about an operation carried out by the The Gadchiroli Revenue Department to sieze 15 tractors carrying sand mined illegally which is taken into custody, with investigation underway.

Despite existing regulations, unauthorized extraction of sand is rampant across various sand ghats. Daily, hundreds of tractor-loads of sand are illicitly mined and transported through routes such as Khukhara and Harladih, often reaching areas like Topchanchi and Dhanbad. A tribal farmer died in Madhya Pradesh’s Singrauli after he was hit by a tractor, allegedly belonging to sand mafia, when he objected to it passing through his agricultural land with grown crop, police said on Monday (September 2, 2024). According to the police, the incident took place on Sunday (September 1, 2024) night in Gannai village in Sarai police station limits, and the police received information on 100 dial helpline at around 8 p.m. about one Indrapal Agariya, 35, being injured in a tractor accident. His family have alleged the tractor belonged to one Lale Vaishya and claimed his driver hit Agariya with the vehicle while carrying sand from the route behind the deceased’s farm. A case has been registered against the driver and owner of the tractor based on the victim family’s allegations.

Dhanlaxmi Company, involved in the sand business in Narsinghpur district, is allegedly bribing administrative officials to avoid action against its illegal operations. Although only 36 sand mines are officially allotted in the district (and just two in Tendukheda tehsil), the company is reportedly deploying influential goons to control several unallotted sand sites. They are illegally collecting ₹700 per trolley as royalty at multiple unauthorized locations along the Narmada River. Despite repeated complaints, the administration has failed to take any action.

The Madhya Pradesh High Court, in response to a PIL by the Narmada Bachao Andolan,  ordered an immediate stay on all sand mining in the Sardar Sarovar Project-affected areas of the Narmada Valley, citing environmental damage and procedural lapses. The Court expressed displeasure at the state government's failure to submit mandatory mining lease details, despite prior orders. It noted that land in the dam submergence zone is owned by the Narmada Valley Development Authority (NVDA) and questioned the legality of lease grants by the mining department in such areas. NBA alleged the illegal mining was harming river ecology, groundwater, reservoir fish, and state revenue. The state's claim of sovereign rights over NVDA lands was rejected by the Court due to the lack of specific information.

There are two different contractors Sahakar Global Company Shahdol and Mahakal Loading Umaria Company which have been assigned different districts for mining sand from in Madhya Pradesh. There has been a history of conflict involving physical violence where the victim contractor from Mahakal Loading Umaria Company says he has been attacked while transporting sand from Amiliya in Shahdol district. Sahakar Company has been given the extraction contract from Podi.

Threats from the sand mining mafia on woman IAS officer's life in Umaria District who is also the district's chief executive officer. She had written to the then Chief Secretary B P Singh. Her letter spoke of the threats that followed her raid in another district Chhatarpur's  Rajnagar area. She had carried out the raid in 2016-17 under Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan. During the raid she and her guard were attacked by Arjun Singh Bundela, who is now planning the attack on her. Arjun Singh Bundela has been in jail since the raid. She fears for her life since she has to appear in the Chattarpur Court for a special hearing which involves Bundela.

In Madhya Pradesh’s Bhind district, journalist Sandeep Sharma, who was investigating illegal sand mining, was mowed down by a truck in what is suspected to be a targeted killing. CCTV footage showed the truck veering directly toward him, raising suspicions of foul play. Sharma had previously reported threats to his life and had submitted a complaint to the police, but no protection was provided. The incident has sparked outrage, with Chief Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan promising strict action. The case highlights the risks faced by journalists probing powerful interests like the illegal sand mining mafia.

description: The Madhya Pradesh Government notified that the MP Minor Minerals Rules, 1996,  constituting district level environmental committees have the power to grant clearance to projects and informed that in addition to MoEF and State Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA), stating that these committees were competent to give environmental clearance for any mining activity in an area less than five hectares (ha). The National Green Tribunal (NGT), while hearing the plea by state government and MP State Mining Corporation  seeking exemption from ban imposed by NGT in August on mining of minor minerals, including sand, without environmental clearance from MoEF. It held that district-level environmental committees formed by the Madhya Pradesh state government to approve mining plans are in conflict with the Central environment laws on sand mining and cannot prevail above them. Only the Ministry of Environment and Forests (MoEF) has the authority to grant environmental clearance.

The contracts of 9 sand mines of Hoshangabad district, 2 of Mandla and 2 of Agar-Malwa have been extended under the transfer system. After the consent of the contractors, the contracts of these mines was extended for one year from 31 March 2020 to 31 March 2021 or till a new contractor comes into the auction process. The state government has directed the Managing Director of the State Mineral Corporation and the concerned District Collector to increase the approved rate per cubic meter by 10 percent in the amount of the contract approved in the financial year 2019-20. No contractor has placed a bid in the current e-tender in Agar-Malwa district. Therefore, the amount per cubic meter should be recovered here at the average rate of the maximum tender rate received in other districts of Ujjain division. The quantity of sand mineral approved for the extended period will be the same as that already contracted. The annual quantity will be divided proportionately over 9 months (excluding monsoon period).
